q: Which of the following is NOT correct about the jurisdiction of the High Court?
options: It controls the subordinate courts within its jurisdiction.
It has the power of judicial review.
It provides advisory opinion to the President of India.
solution:
The correct answer is It provides advisory opinion to the President of India.

Key Points

• The High Courts of India are the highest courts of appellate jurisdiction in each State and Union Territory of India.

• Judges in a high court are appointed by the President of India in consultation with the chief justice of India and the governor of the state under Art 217 of the Constitution but through subsequent judicial interpretations, the primacy of the appointment process is in the hands of the Judicial Collegium.

• High courts are headed by a chief justice.

• The chief justices rank fourteenth (within their respective states) and seventeenth (outside their respective states) on the Indian order of precedence.

• The number of judges in a court is decided by dividing the average institution of main cases during the last five years by the national average, or the average rate of disposal of main cases per judge per year in that high court, whichever is higher.

• The judge of High court retires at the age of 62.

• According to Article 124(2) of the Constitution, the age of retirement for Supreme Court judges is 65.

• As per Article 217(1) of the Constitution, High Court judges retire at 62.

• Initially, the retirement age of High Court judges was 60, which was later in 1963 increased to 62 through the 15th constitutional amendment Bill.

• The idea of increasing the age of retirement for judges has been mooted for decades as a solution for dealing with mounting pendency of cases and judicial vacancies.

• It has also been discussed in the context of ensuring serving judges do not look for post-retirement jobs from the executive.

• Attorney General for India K K Venugopal has been one of the vocal advocates of increasing tenure of the judges, and has consistently spoken about it at every farewell of Supreme Court judges since 2017.

q: Which of the following jurisdictions of the Supreme Court allows it to settle disputes between the centre and state and amongst states?
solution:
Correct Answer Original

The power of the Supreme Court of India to decide the disputes between the Centre and States falls under Original Jurisdiction.

Key PointsOriginal Jurisdiction

• As a Federal court, the Supreme Court decides disputes between different units of the Indian Federation.

• More elaborately, any dispute between:

• The Centre and one or more states

• The Centre and any state or states on one side and one or more states on the other

• Between two or more states

• In the above federal disputes, the Supreme Court has exclusive original jurisdiction.

• Hence, option 4 is the correct answer.

Important Points

Appellate Jurisdiction

• The Supreme Court is primarily a court of appeal and hears appeals against the judgments of the lower courts.

• It enjoys a wide appellate jurisdiction which can be classified under four heads:

• Appeals in constitutional matters

• Appeals in civil matters

• Appeals in criminal matters

• Appeals by special leave

Advisory Jurisdiction

• The Constitution under Article 143 authorizes the President to seek the opinion of the Supreme Court in the two categories of matters:

• On any question of law or fact of public importance which has arisen or which is likely to arise

• On any dispute arising out of any pre-constitution treaty, agreement, covenant, engagement, sanador other similar instruments

• or the use of wells, tanks, bathing ghats, roads, and places of public resort maintained wholly or partly out of State funds or dedicated to the use of the general public

q: How many types of writs can be issued under Article 32 and 226 of the Constitution of India?
solution:
The correct answer is Option 3.

Key Points

• Under the Constitution of India, Article 32 provides for the right to constitutional remedies, while Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs. The following are the different types of writs that can be issued under these articles:

• Habeas corpus - to produce a person who is under illegal detention

• Mandamus - to compel a public official or body to perform a duty

• Prohibition - to prohibit a lower court or tribunal from exceeding its jurisdiction

• Certiorari - to quash the order of a lower court or tribunal

• Quo warranto - to question the authority or legality of a person holding a public office

• Thus, a total of five types of writs can be issued under Article 32 and 226 of the Constitution of India.

Additional Information

• Article 32 of the Indian Constitution guarantees the right to constitutional remedies to every citizen of India.

• This article empowers the citizens to approach the Supreme Court of India to seek enforcement of their fundamental rights.

• The Supreme Court has the power to issue writs, including habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, and quo warranto, for the enforcement of fundamental rights and for any other purpose.

• The right to move the Supreme Court under Article 32 is considered as a fundamental right in itself, and any law or action that violates the fundamental rights can be challenged under this article.

• This article ensures that the citizens have a direct access to the Supreme Court, which is the highest court of the land, to seek justice and protection of their rights.

• Article 32 is often regarded as the most important and valuable provision in the Indian Constitution, as it provides a powerful mechanism to protect the fundamental rights of the citizens and to ensure that the government acts in accordance with the Constitution.

• Article 226 of the Constitution of India empowers the High Courts to issue writs for the enforcement of fundamental rights and for any other purpose.

• The High Court, being the highest court in a state, has wide-ranging powers to exercise judicial review over the decisions of inferior courts, tribunals, and other authorities within its territorial jurisdiction.

q:
Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding the Multi-State Co-operative Societies (Amendment) Bill, 2022?

A. The Lok Sabha referred this Bill to the joint committee of parliament comprising 21 members from the Lower House and 10 from the Upper House.

B. This Bill also proposed to establish a ‘Cooperative Election Authority’ to bring electoral reforms.

C. The Bill also has a Section — 63A that relates to ‘establishment of the Cooperative Rehabilitation, Reconstruction and Development Fund’ for revival of ‘sick multi-state cooperative societies’.
solution:
The correct answer is Option 3.

Key Points

•

The Bill amends the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act, 2002.

•

It establishes the Co-operative Election Authority to conduct and supervise elections to the boards of multi-state co-operative societies. A multi-state co-operative society will require prior permission of government authorities before the redemption of their shareholding.

•

A Co-operative Rehabilitation, Reconstruction and Development Fund will be established for the revival of sick multi-state co-operative societies. The Fund will be financed through contributions by profitable multi-state co-operative societies.

•

The Bill allows state co-operative societies to merge into an existing multi-state co-operative society, subject to the respective state laws.

Additional Information Key Features

• Election of board members:

• Under the Act, elections to the board of a multi-state co-operative society are conducted by its existing board.

• The Bill amends this to specify that the central government will establish the Co-operative Election Authority to:

• conduct such elections,

• supervise, direct, and control the preparation of electoral rolls, and

• perform other prescribed functions.

• The Authority will consist of a chairperson, vice-chairperson, and up to three members appointed by the central government on the recommendations of a selection committee.

• Amalgamation of co-operative societies:

• The Act provides for the amalgamation and division of multi-state co-operative societies.

• This can be done by passing a resolution at a general meeting with at least two-thirds of the members, present and voting.

• The Bill allows state co-operative societies to merge into an existing multi-state co-operative society, subject to the respective state laws.

• At least two-thirds of the members of the co-operative society present and voting at a general meeting must pass a resolution to allow such a merger.

• Fund for sick co-operative societies:

• The Bill establishes the Co-operative Rehabilitation, Reconstruction and Development Fund for revival of sick multi-state co-operative societies. A sick multi-state co-operative society is one that has:

• (i) accumulated losses equal to or exceeding the total of its paid-up capital, free reserves, and surpluses, and

• (ii) suffered cash losses in the past two financial years.

• The central government may prepare a scheme for rehabilitation and reconstruction of the society. Multi-state co-operative societies that are in profit for the preceding three financial years shall finance the Fund.

• They will deposit either one crore rupees or one percent of their net profit into the Fund, whichever is less.

• Restriction on redemption of government shareholding:

• The Act provides that the shares held in a multi-state co-operative society by certain government authorities can be redeemed based on the bye-laws of the society.

• These government authorities include:

• (i) the central government,

• (ii) state governments,

• (iii) the National Co-operative Development Corporation,

• (iv) any corporation owned or controlled by the government, or

• (v) any government company.

• The Bill amends this to provide that any shares held by the central and state governments cannot be redeemed without their prior approval.

• Redressal of complaints:

• ​As per the Bill, the central government will appoint one or more Co-operative Ombudsman with territorial jurisdiction.

• The Ombudsman shall inquire into complaints made by members of multi-state co-operative societies regarding:

• (i) their deposits,

• (ii) equitable benefits of the society’s functioning, or

• (iii) issues affecting the individual rights of the members.

• The Ombudsman shall complete the process of inquiry and adjudication within three months from the receipt of the complaint. Appeals against the directions of the Ombudsman may be filed with the Central Registrar (who is appointed by the central government) within a month.

q:
Which of the following statements are correct regarding the Supreme Court judgement on validity of 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act?

A. The Supreme Court of India’s Constitutional Bench for this case consisted of 5 judges.

B. The Constitutional Bench upholds the 10% of EWS reservation with 3-2 majority.

C. As per the Supreme Court judgement, the 103rd Constitutional Amendment is valid although it is violating the Basic Structure of the Indian Constitution.
solution:
The correct answer is A and B only.

Key Points

• The 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act was passed in January 2019 and it provided for a 10% reservation in government jobs and educational institutions for economically weaker sections (EWS) of the society who are not covered under existing reservations for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and Other Backward Classes.

• The main argument against the Amendment was that it violates the basic structure of the Constitution, which includes the principle of equality and the principle of reservation as enshrined in the Constitution.

• In a landmark judgement delivered on May 5, 2021, a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court upheld the validity of the 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act.

• The Bench comprised of 5 Justices Ashok Bhushan, L Nageswara Rao, S Abdul Nazeer, Hemant Gupta, and S Ravindra Bhat.

• The Supreme Court held that the 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act does not violate the basic structure of the Constitution.

• The Court held that the principle of reservation is not an immutable feature of the Constitution and that the State has the power to provide for reservation to any socially and educationally backward class of citizens.

• The Court also held that the 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act is a valid exercise of the State's power to provide for reservation.

• The Constitutional Bench upholds the 10% of EWS reservation with 3-2 majority.

• The Supreme Court also held that the 10% reservation for EWS provided under the 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act is not limited to any particular religion or caste and is available to all those who are economically backward and do not fall within the scope of the existing reservations for SCs, STs, and OBCs.

q: Which of the following amendments to the Indian Constitution made the Right to Property a Legal Right in place of a Fundamental Right?
solution:
The correct answer is 44th. Key Points

• The Right to Property was removed as a Fundamental Right from the Indian Constitution by the 44th Amendment in 1978. It was changed into a legal right under Article 300A in Part XII of the Constitution.

• The Right to Property underwent numerous changes throughout history in the Indian Constitution before it was eventually downgraded to a legal right. It started as a Fundamental Right:

• Post-independence - The original Constitution of India, when it came into effect in 1950, recognized the Right to Property as a Fundamental Right under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31. Article 19(1)(f) allowed citizens to acquire, hold, and dispose of property, while Article 31 provided that "no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law."

• First Amendment, 1951 - In response to significant land reform initiatives and intended to prevent the judiciary from undermining those policies, the First Amendment was introduced, which placed restrictions on the Right to Property.

• Fourth Amendment, 1955 - This amendment further reduced the right to property in response to a series of court decisions that favored landowners' rights to fair compensation over the state's rights to carry out land and tenancy reforms.

• Over time, several other amendments were made affecting the Right to Property: the Seventeenth Amendment of 1964, the Twenty-Fifth Amendment of 1971, the Thirty-Ninth Amendment of 1975, among others.

• Forty-Fourth Amendment, 1978 - Eventually, the Right to Property was removed as a Fundamental Right. The 44th Amendment, enacted by the Janata Party which came into power in 1977, downgraded the right to a constitutional/legal right. The amendment also introduced a new article, Article 300A, which provided: "No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law." This means that the government can deprive a citizen of private property, but it has to be as per a valid law.

• This change made it possible for the government to implement land reform and redistribution policies without fear of them being declared unconstitutional by the courts. The Right to Property is now protected under the Indian Constitution as a legal right, not as a Fundamental Right. This means that while an individual still has the right to property, it is not an absolute right and can be regulated by the government.

Out of these, 12 are nominated by the President from persons having special knowledge or practical experience in the fields of literature, science, art, and social service, and the rest represent the States and Union territories.

• Article 81: This Article provides for the composition of the Lok Sabha. The House of the People or Lok Sabha consists of representatives directly elected by people of the territorial constituencies in the states and Union territories. As per the amendment of 1977, the Lok Sabha shall consist of not more than 552 members - up to 530 members to represent the territorial constituencies in the States, up to 20 members from Union Territories.

q:
Which of the following pairs is/are correctly matched regarding the terminology used in the Parliament?

A. Appropriation Bill - A Money Bill passed for providing for the withdrawal or appropriation from and out of the Consolidated Fund of India

B. Demand for Grants - Earmarking of budgetary allocation for meeting only planned expenditure of a Ministry/Department

C. Short Duration Discussion - For raising a discussion on a matter of urgent public importance for which a notice has to be given by a Member and supported by 50 Members
solution:
The correct answer is A only. Key Points

• A. Appropriation Bill - The Appropriation Bill is indeed a Money Bill passed for providing for the withdrawal or appropriation from and out of the Consolidated Fund of India. Therefore, this option is correctly matched.

• B. Demand for Grants and C. Short Duration Discussion - are incorrectly paired in the context provided.

• The "Demands for Grants" are the estimates of expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India, presented to the Lok Sabha for its approval. The demands are presented ministry-wise.

• A "Short Duration Discussion" in the Indian parliament refers to a discussion on a matter of urgent public importance, which can be raised with prior notice, but it does not need to be supported by 50 members, so again the pairing is incorrect.

• So, based on the given pairs, the correct answer is "A only".

Additional Information

• Money Bill: Any bill that pertains to taxation and government finances is classified as a Money Bill under Article 110. The Speaker of the Lok Sabha holds the authority to decide whether a financial bill is a Money Bill or not. In the case of Money Bills, the Rajya Sabha (Upper House) has limited powers—all amendments recommended by Rajya Sabha are not binding on Lok Sabha.

• Ordinance: Under Article 123, the President of India is empowered to issue ordinances when Parliament is not in session, and immediate legislative action is needed. However, such an ordinance must be approved by the Parliament within six weeks of its next session.

• Question Hour: This is the first hour of a parliamentary sitting/session where Members of Parliament ask questions to ministers and hold them accountable for the functioning of their ministries.

• Zero Hour: Unlike the Question Hour, the Zero Hour is not mentioned in any rules of procedure. Thus, it is an informal but powerful tool available to the members of the Parliament to raise matters of great importance without any prior notice.

• Quorum (Article 100): This refers to the minimum number of Members of Parliament that must be present to make the proceedings of that House valid. In India, the quorum to conduct a meeting of either House of Parliament is one-tenth of the total number of seats in that House.

• Powers, Privileges, etc. of Parliament Members (Article 105): According to this article, the Parliament and its members and committees have powers and privileges that are necessary for the exercise of their responsibilities. No Member of Parliament can be held liable in any court for anything that is said, or any vote given, in Parliament or its committee meetings.

• Motion of No Confidence: This is a statement or vote that states or proposes that a government must be called into account. A motion of no confidence mandates the government to prove its majority in the house.

• Private Member's Bill: Any bill introduced by a Member of Parliament who is not a minister is called a private member's bill. These bills are treated the same as other public bills, but in practicality, they have little chance of being passed due to lower precedence on the legislative agenda.

• Cut Motions: These are objections raised in Lok Sabha to the demand made for grants, essentially objections to the amount of financial expenditure.

q: The Indian Constitution was adopted on which of the following dates?
solution:
The correct answer is 26th November 1949.

Key Points

• Indian Constitution:-

• The Constitution of India is the supreme law of India.

• It lays down the framework that demarcates the political principles, establishes the structure, procedures, powers, and duties of the government institutions, and sets out the fundamental rights, directive principles, and duties of citizens.

• The Indian Constitution is the longest written constitution of any sovereign country in the world.

• It was drafted by the Constituent Assembly of India, which was elected by the elected members of the provincial assemblies.

• Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was appointed the chairman of the drafting committee, and he is often recognized as the principal architect of the constitution.

• The constitution was adopted by the Constituent Assembly of India on 26th November 1949 and officially came into effect on 26th January 1950, a date celebrated as Republic Day in India.

• The constitution declared India to be a sovereign, socialist, secular, and democratic republic, and it assures its citizens of justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity.

• The Indian Constitution is a comprehensive document with a preamble and 448 articles, which are grouped into 25 parts with 12 schedules and five appendices.

• It envisages a parliamentary form of government, which is federal in structure with unitary features.

• The contemporary constitution can be divided into two parts—union and states. The union part contains the powers and functions of union executives, parliament, and judiciary, while the state part has the same for states.

q: Which of the following committees recommended for the inclusion of fundamental duties in the Constitution of India?
solution:
The correct answer is Swaran Singh Committee.

Key Points

• The Swaran Singh Committee was established in 1976 under the leadership of Sardar Swaran Singh, an Indian Politician.

• The committee was specifically constituted to study and suggest changes to the Constitution in relation to the concept of fundamental duties. It was the Swaran Singh Committee that suggested adding a new part outlining citizen duties.

• As a result of this committee's recommendations, the 42nd Amendment to the Constitution in 1976 included the new Part IVA, which specified the fundamental duties of Indian citizens. It comprises Article 51A from (a) to (k).

• The fundamental duties include tenets like respect for the national flag, the constitution, and institutions, promoting brotherhood, protecting the environment, and upholding scientific temper among others.

• The primary aim behind the inclusion of the Fundamental Duties by this committee was to create a balance of rights and duties in the constitution, obliging citizens to act responsibly and assist in maintaining the spirit of democracy in India.

Additional Information

• Sarkaria Commission:

• The Sarkaria Commission was established in 1983 by the central government of India.

• The Commission was set up to examine the relationship and balance of power between state and central governments in the country and suggest changes within the framework of the Constitution.

• It made 247 recommendations to improve the efficiency, effectiveness, and balance between the various levels of government in India.

• The report of the Sarkaria Commission is the first and the most comprehensive attempt to review Centre-State relationship.

• Rajamannar Committee:

• The Rajamannar Committee was constituted by the government of Tamil Nadu in 1969.

• Its task was to examine the entire question concerning state autonomy and the Centre-State relations.

• The committee recommended a drastic overhaul of India’s federal system, with suggestions for the constitution to emerge as a truly federal one rather than quasi-federal.

• The need for such changes arose because of the contention that centralization of power diminishes the effectiveness of regional governments.

• Balwant Rai Mehta Committee:

• The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee was a committee appointed by the Government of India in 1957.

• The aim of this Committee was to examine the working of the Community Development Programme (1952) and the National Extension Service (1953) and to suggest measures for their better working.

• Significantly, their recommendations led to the birth of Panchayati Raj Institutions in India, outlining a three-tier system, including village, block, and district levels.

• The report of the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee is considered a landmark in the evolution of local self-government (Panchayati Raj) institutions in India.

q: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT about the Directive Principles of State Policy?
options: They promote welfare of individuals. Hence, they are personal and individualistic.
These have moral and political sanctions.
They aim at establishing social and economic democracy in the country.
They are positive, as they require the State to do certain things.
solution:
The correct answer is They promote welfare of individuals. Hence, they are personal and individualistic.

Key Points

• The Directive Principles of State Policy of India are the guidelines or principles given to the institutes for governing India and are provided in Part IV of the Constitution of India.

• Directive Principles of State Policy aim to create social and economic conditions under which the citizens can lead a good life.

• They also aim to establish social and economic democracy through a welfare state. Directive principles are classified under the following categories; economic, socialistic, political, executive, justice and legal, administrative, environmental, protection of monuments, peace, and security.

Hence, it can be said that the Directive Principles of State Policy are fundamental for the Governance of the state.

Additional Information

• Features of DPSPs

• The phrase ‘Directive Principles of State Policy’ denotes the ideals that the State should keep in mind while formulating policies and enacting laws.

• These are the constitutional instructions or recommendations to the State in legislative, executive, and administrative matters. According to Article 36, the term ‘State’ in Part IV has the same meaning as in Part III dealing with Fundamental Rights.

• Therefore, it includes the legislative and executive organs of the central and state governments, all local authorities, and all other public authorities in the country.

• The Directive Principles resemble the ‘Instrument of Instructions’ enumerated in the Government of India Act of 1935.

• In the words of Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, ‘the Directive Principles are like the instrument of instructions, which were issued to the Governor-General and to the Governors of the colonies of India by the British Government under the Government of India Act of 1935. What is called Directive Principles is merely another name for the instrument of instruction. The only difference is that they are instructions to the legislature and the executive’.

• The Directive Principles constitute a very comprehensive economic, social and political program for a modern democratic State.

• They aim at realizing the high ideals of justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity as outlined in the Preamble to the Constitution.

• They embody the concept of a ‘welfare state’ and not that of a ‘police state’, which existed during the colonial era3. In brief, they seek to establish economic and social democracy in the country.

• The Directive Principles are non-justiciable in nature, that is, they are not legally enforceable by the courts for their violation.

• Therefore, the government (Central, state, and local) cannot be compelled to implement them.

• Nevertheless, the Constitution (Article 37) itself says that these principles are fundamental in the governance of the country and it shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws.

• The Directive Principles, though nonjusticiable in nature, help the courts in examining and determining the constitutional validity of a law.

• The Supreme Court has ruled many times that in determining the constitutionality of any law if a court finds that the law in question seeks to give effect to a Directive Principle, it may consider such law to be ‘reasonable’ in relation to Article 14 (equality before law) or Article 19 (six freedoms) and thus save such law from unconstitutionality.

q: Which of the following is NOT a Fundamental Duty of the Indian citizens?

q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution provides that the State must secure a social order to promote the welfare of people?

Additional Information

• Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)

• It emphasizes that the principles laid down are fundamental in the governance of the country.

• It directs the State to ensure that the citizens, men and women equally, have the right to an adequate means of livelihood.

• This article defines the term "State" in the context of DPSP.

q: Which Article of the Constitution of India provides that 'there shall be a Vice President of India'?
solution:
The correct answer is Article 63.

Key Points

• Article 63

• Article 63 of the Indian Constitution states that "There shall be a vice president of India."

• The vice president acts as president in the absence of the president due to death, resignation, impeachment, or other situations.

• The vice president of India is also ex officio chairperson of the Rajya Sabha. When a bill is introduced in Rajya Sabha, the vice president decides whether it is a financial bill or not.

• If he is of the opinion, a bill introduced in the Rajya Sabha is a money bill, he would refer the case to the Speaker of the Lok Sabha for deciding it.

Additional Information

• Article 61

• The process for the impeachment of the President is outlined in Article 61 of the Indian Constitution.

• Either House of Parliament may file the impeachment accusations.

• The President must be notified 14 days in advance, and these allegations must be signed by one-fourth of the House members who framed them.

• The other House, which is tasked with conducting an investigation into the allegations, receives the impeachment resolution when it has been approved by a two-thirds majority of the entire membership of that House.

• The President has the right to show up and be represented during such an investigation.

• The President is removed from office as of the date the resolution is passed if the other House concurs with the accusations and approves the impeachment resolution with a two-thirds majority of its members.

• Impeachment is a quasi-judicial process in Parliament as a result.

• In this context, it is important to keep in mind two things:

• nominated members of either House of Parliament may take part in the impeachment of the President even though they did not cast a ballot in his election;

• and elected members of state legislative assemblies and the union territories of Delhi and Puducherry may not, even though they cast a ballot in the President's election.

• Article 65

• Article 65 deals with the Vice-President acting as President or discharging the functions of the President in the event of a vacancy.

q: Which of the following features of the Indian Constitution was borrowed from Irish Constitution?

q: Which Article in the fundamental duty applies, when a construction worker takes his 8-year son to the site rather than sending him to school?

• It is a fundamental right under Article 21A of the Indian Constitution.

• The Act ensures that children have access to quality education without discrimination and establishes norms for school infrastructure, teacher-student ratio, and curriculum.

• Child labor refers to the employment of children in a manner that deprives them of their childhood, education, or is harmful to their health and development.

• The Child Labor (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986, and its amendments prohibit the employment of children below 14 years in hazardous occupations and processes.

• Efforts to eliminate child labor involve providing education and support to families to ensure children attend school instead of engaging in work.

q: Which of following is NOT a device of parliamentary proceedings?
solution:
The correct answer is Full-day discussion.

Key Points

• Full-day discussion is not a recognized device of parliamentary proceedings in India.

• Indian Parliament has specific mechanisms for discussions such as Half-an-hour discussion, Zero-hour discussion, and Two-hour (short) discussion.

• These mechanisms are structured to ensure organized and efficient proceedings within the Parliament.

• The concept of a "Full-day discussion" does not exist as a formal parliamentary procedure in India.

Additional Information

• Half-an-hour discussion

• It is a device in the Indian Parliament where members can raise a matter of public importance, which requires an oral answer from the concerned minister.

• This discussion takes place for half an hour, typically at the end of the day's session.

• It allows members to seek clarification on specific issues from the ministers.

• Zero-hour discussion

• It is an informal device available to the members of the Indian Parliament to raise matters without any prior notice.

• It starts immediately after the Question Hour and lasts until the agenda for the day is taken up.

• Members can raise urgent matters of public importance during this time.

• Two-hour (short) discussion

• This device allows for a discussion on a matter of urgent public importance for a duration of two hours.

• No formal motion is moved and no voting takes place at the end of the discussion.

• The aim is to allow members to express their views and enable the government to clarify its position on the issue.

• Ordinances allow the government to take swift action on matters of urgency without waiting for Parliament to convene.

• Article 123 of the Indian Constitution:

• Article 123 grants the President the power to promulgate ordinances during the recess of Parliament.

• This provision ensures that the executive can address urgent issues without legislative delays.

• Ordinances must be laid before both Houses of Parliament and require their approval to become permanent laws.

• This power is subject to judicial review to prevent misuse and ensure adherence to constitutional principles.

• Separation of Powers:

• The Indian Constitution follows the principle of separation of powers among the executive, legislature, and judiciary.

• The President's ordinance-making power represents an overlap between the executive and legislative functions.

• This power is exercised with checks and balances to prevent abuse and ensure accountability.

q: In which of the following years was the Election Commission of India founded?

5 years or up to the age of 60 years
6 years or up to the age of 60 years
solution:
The correct answer is 6 years or up to the age of 65 years.

Key Points

• The tenure of the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) is 6 years or up to the age of 65 years, whichever is earlier.

• The Chief Election Commissioner can be removed from office only through impeachment by Parliament for proven misbehavior or incapacity.

• The CEC and other Election Commissioners have the same powers, salary, allowances, and other perquisites as are available to a judge of the Supreme Court of India.

• The concept of an independent Election Commission was introduced to ensure free and fair elections in India, as per the provisions of Article 324 of the Indian Constitution.

Additional Information

• Election Commission of India (ECI)

• The Election Commission of India is an autonomous constitutional authority responsible for administering election processes in India at both the national and state levels.

• The body administers elections to the Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, and State Legislative Assemblies, as well as the offices of the President and Vice President in the country.

• The Election Commission operates under the authority of Constitution per Article 324, and subsequently enacted Representation of the People Act.

• The commission has the powers to monitor the election process, including the preparation of electoral rolls, ensuring the model code of conduct, and scrutinizing election expenses of candidates.

• Chief Election Commissioner (CEC)

• The Chief Election Commissioner heads the Election Commission of India and oversees the entire electoral process.

• Appointed by the President of India, the CEC ensures that the election process is conducted in a free, fair, and impartial manner.

• The CEC can only be removed through a process similar to that of a judge of the Supreme Court, which requires a two-thirds majority in Parliament.

• The CEC’s role is critical in maintaining the sanctity of the democratic process in India.

q: Ranjana Prakash Desai who became the first woman chairperson of the Press Council of India originally worked in which of the following organs of the government?
solution:
The correct answer is Judiciary.

Key Points

• Ranjana Prakash Desai is a former judge of the Supreme Court of India.

• She has served in the judiciary system and has made significant contributions to the legal field.

• As a judge, she has been involved in several landmark judgments and cases.

• Her appointment as the chairperson of the Press Council of India marks a significant milestone as she is the first woman to hold this position.

Additional Information

• Judiciary:

• The judiciary is one of the three pillars of democracy, the other two being the legislature and the executive.

• It is responsible for interpreting the laws, ensuring justice, and maintaining the rule of law in the country.

• The judiciary comprises various levels of courts, including the Supreme Court, High Courts, and lower courts.

• Judges in the judiciary system play a crucial role in adjudicating disputes, protecting rights, and upholding the Constitution.

• Press Council of India (PCI):

• The Press Council of India is a statutory body established under the Press Council Act of 1978.

• It aims to preserve the freedom of the press and maintain and improve the standards of newspapers and news agencies in India.

• The PCI acts as a watchdog of the press, ensuring ethical standards and addressing complaints against the press.

• The chairperson of the PCI is typically a retired judge of the Supreme Court or a High Court.

• Supreme Court of India:

• The Supreme Court of India is the highest judicial authority in the country.

• It has the power of judicial review, which allows it to invalidate laws and executive actions that are inconsistent with the Constitution.

• It comprises the Chief Justice of India and a number of other judges as prescribed by law.

• The Supreme Court ensures the protection of fundamental rights and resolves disputes between the central and state governments.

q: Which of the following is NOT a feature of the Constitution of India?
solution:
The correct answer is Dual Citizenship.

Key Points

• The Constitution of India does not provide for dual citizenship.

• India follows a single citizenship policy, which means that a person is a citizen of India only and not of any state individually.

• Dual citizenship could lead to complications in matters of loyalty and allegiance, thus the Indian Constitution avoids it.

• Other countries may allow dual citizenship, but India mandates renouncing Indian citizenship upon acquiring foreign nationality.

Additional Information

• Universal Adult Franchise

• It is a fundamental principle of democracy where all adult citizens have the right to vote without any discrimination.

• In India, it was adopted with the commencement of the Constitution on January 26, 1950.

• It ensures equality and inclusiveness in the electoral process.

• Every citizen above the age of 18 has the right to vote in elections to the Lok Sabha and the Legislative Assemblies.

• Independent Judiciary

• It refers to a judiciary that is free from any influence or control by the executive or the legislature.

• The Indian Constitution ensures the independence of the judiciary through various provisions such as the security of tenure, fixed service conditions, and restrictions on practice after retirement.

• Judicial independence is crucial for the fair administration of justice and upholding the rule of law.

• The Supreme Court and High Courts in India are the guardians of the Constitution and are empowered to review laws and executive actions.

• Blend of Rigidity & Flexibility

• The Indian Constitution is a unique blend of rigidity and flexibility.

• Some parts of the Constitution can be amended by a simple majority, while others require a special majority or ratification by half of the state legislatures.

• This blend allows the Constitution to adapt to changing needs while preserving its core principles.

• Article 368 of the Constitution provides for the amendment process.

q: The Epidemic Diseases (Amendment) Ordinance, 2020 amended which of the following Acts?
solution:
The correct answer is The Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897.

Key Points

• The Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 was enacted to provide for better prevention of the spread of dangerous epidemic diseases.

• The Act gives special powers to state and central governments to take measures necessary to prevent the outbreak or spread of an epidemic.

• The Epidemic Diseases (Amendment) Ordinance, 2020 was introduced to include protections for healthcare personnel combatting epidemic diseases.

• The Ordinance also provides for stricter penalties for acts of violence against healthcare service personnel and damage to property during epidemics.

Additional Information

• Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897

• The Act was passed by the British colonial government in India in 1897 in response to the bubonic plague outbreak in Mumbai (then Bombay).

• The Act allows the central and state governments to take special measures and prescribe regulations to prevent the spread of epidemic diseases.

• The Act also provides the legal framework for the implementation of containment measures such as quarantine, isolation, and restrictions on the movement of people.

• The Act has been invoked several times in India, including during the outbreaks of H1N1 influenza (swine flu), dengue, and COVID-19.

• The Epidemic Diseases (Amendment) Ordinance, 2020

• The Ordinance was promulgated by the President of India on April 22, 2020, in response to the COVID-19 pandemic.

• It amends the Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 to include protections for healthcare service personnel combating epidemic diseases.

• The Ordinance defines "healthcare service personnel" to include healthcare professionals, nurses, paramedical workers, and any other person empowered under the Act to take measures to prevent the outbreak or spread of an epidemic disease.

• It provides for imprisonment and fines for acts of violence against healthcare service personnel and damage to property during epidemics.

• Other Important Terminologies

• Quarantine: A restriction on the movement of people and goods intended to prevent the spread of disease or pests.

• Isolation: The separation of people who are infected with a contagious disease from those who are healthy to prevent the spread of the disease.

• Containment Measures: Strategies and actions taken to prevent the spread of a disease within a community, including quarantine, isolation, and restrictions on movement.

q: Part IV A of the Indian Constitution was inserted in the Indian Constitution through  Constitutional Amendment Act.
solution:
The correct answer is 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act.

Key Points

• The 42nd Amendment Act, also known as the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, was enacted during the Emergency period in India.

• It is considered one of the most comprehensive amendments to the Indian Constitution and was brought in by the Indira Gandhi government.

• This amendment made significant changes to the Constitution, including the insertion of Part IV A, which deals with the Fundamental Duties of the citizens.

• The 42nd Amendment also attempted to reduce the power of the judiciary and increase the power of the Parliament.

Additional Information

• Part IV A (Fundamental Duties)

• Part IV A was added to the Constitution of India by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.

• It consists of Article 51A which enumerates the Fundamental Duties of the citizens of India.

• These duties are inspired by the Constitution of the former Soviet Union and aim to remind the citizens of their moral obligations towards the nation.

• There are currently 11 Fundamental Duties listed in Article 51A.

• 42nd Amendment Act, 1976

• Known as a "mini-Constitution" due to its wide-ranging amendments.

• It made extensive changes to the Preamble, Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles, and the structure of the executive and judiciary.

• This amendment curtailed the power of the judiciary and strengthened the central government.

• Many of the provisions of this amendment were later undone by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978.

• Emergency Period

• The Emergency in India was declared by President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed upon the advice of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi from 1975 to 1977.

• This period is considered one of the most controversial times in Indian political history, marked by the suspension of elections and civil liberties.

• The 42nd Amendment was passed during this period, and it significantly altered the balance of power between the executive, legislature, and judiciary.

q: Who among the following is NOT a member of the National Human Rights Commission?
options: Former Chief Justice of the High Court
Former Chief Justice of the Supreme Court
Former Judge of the Supreme Court
solution:
The correct answer is District Magistrate.

Key Points

• The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) is a statutory body established under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.

• The NHRC consists of a Chairperson and members who are appointed by the President of India.

• The Chairperson of the NHRC is a former Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of India.

• Members of the NHRC include former Chief Justices and Judges of the Supreme Court, as well as other eminent persons with knowledge and experience in human rights.

Additional Information

• National Human Rights Commission (NHRC)

• The NHRC is responsible for the protection and promotion of human rights in India.

• Human rights include the rights to life, liberty, equality, and dignity of individuals guaranteed by the Indian Constitution and enforceable by courts in India.

• The NHRC investigates complaints of human rights violations, conducts inquiries, and makes recommendations to the government.

• The NHRC also engages in human rights education, awareness, and training programs.

• District Magistrate

• A District Magistrate (DM) is an administrative officer of an Indian state, responsible for maintaining law and order, implementing government policies, and overseeing the administration of a district.

• The DM is not a member of the NHRC.

• Former Chief Justice of the High Court

• A former Chief Justice of a High Court can be appointed as a member of the NHRC.

• Former Chief Justice of the Supreme Court

• The Chairperson of the NHRC is a former Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of India.

• Former Judge of the Supreme Court

• A former Judge of the Supreme Court can be appointed as a member of the NHRC.

q: Which committee recommended Constitutional recognition for the local government bodies in 1989?
solution:
The correct answer is PK Thungon Committee.

Key Points

• The PK Thungon Committee was formed in 1988 to review the working of the Panchayati Raj institutions.

• The committee recommended Constitutional recognition for the local government bodies.

• It suggested the establishment of three-tier Panchayati Raj system in the states.

• The recommendations led to the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments, which were enacted in 1992 and came into effect in 1993.

Additional Information

• Panchayati Raj System

• The Panchayati Raj system is a form of local self-government in rural India.

• It was introduced by the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1992.

• The system consists of three levels: the Gram Panchayat (village level), the Panchayat Samiti (block level), and the Zila Parishad (district level).

• This system aims to decentralize the administration and promote local governance.

• 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act

• It was enacted in 1992 and came into effect on 24 April 1993.

• This amendment provided a constitutional status to the Panchayati Raj institutions.

• It introduced Article 243 to 243O in Part IX of the Constitution.

• The Act mandates the establishment of Panchayats at the village, intermediate, and district levels in all states and Union territories.

• It also provides for the reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and women.

• 74th Constitutional Amendment Act

• It was enacted in 1992 and came into effect on 1 June 1993.

• This amendment provided a constitutional status to the Urban Local Bodies (ULBs).

• It introduced Article 243P to 243ZG in Part IXA of the Constitution.

• The Act mandates the establishment of Municipalities in urban areas.

• It also provides for the reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and women.

q: The  of every state unfurls the flag in its capital on the Republic Day.
solution:
The correct answer is Governor.

Key Points

• The Governor is the constitutional head of a state in India, appointed by the President of India.

• On Republic Day, the Governor unfurls the national flag at the state capital as part of the official celebration.

• The Governor's role is to represent the central government in the state and act according to the advice of the state's Council of Ministers.

• The Governor has various powers and functions including legislative, executive, and discretionary powers as outlined in the Constitution of India.

Additional Information

• Republic Day

• Republic Day in India is celebrated on January 26th every year to honor the date on which the Constitution of India came into effect in 1950.

• It marks the transition of India from a British Dominion to a republic.

• The day is celebrated with grand parades in the national capital, New Delhi, and state capitals, showcasing India's defense capability, cultural and social heritage.

• Role of the Governor

• The Governor is the nominal executive head of the state, functioning as a representative of the President of India.

• The Governor's powers and duties include summoning and proroguing the state legislature, granting pardons, and appointing the Chief Minister.

• Governors can also reserve bills passed by the state legislature for the President's consideration.

• Chief Minister

• The Chief Minister is the head of the government in a state and is responsible for running the state administration.

• They are appointed by the Governor and are usually the leader of the majority party in the state legislature.

• The Chief Minister advises the Governor on various matters related to the state's governance.

q: The Upper House of a State Legislature is known as the _.
solution:
The correct answer is Vidhan Parishad.

Key Points

• The Vidhan Parishad is the Upper House of the State Legislature in India.

• It is similar to the Rajya Sabha, which is the Upper House of the Parliament of India.

• Not all states in India have a Vidhan Parishad; it exists only in a few states like Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, and Telangana.

• Members of the Vidhan Parishad are not directly elected by the public; they are elected by members of the Legislative Assembly, graduates, teachers, and local authority members.

Additional Information

• Rajya Sabha

• The Rajya Sabha is the Upper House of the Parliament of India.

• It represents the states and union territories of India.

• Members of the Rajya Sabha are elected by the elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies, and by the members of the Electoral college for Union Territories, using a single transferable vote system.

• The Rajya Sabha is a permanent body and is not subject to dissolution, but one-third of its members retire every two years.

• Lok Sabha

• The Lok Sabha is the Lower House of the Parliament of India.

• Members of the Lok Sabha are directly elected by the people of India through general elections held every five years.

• The Lok Sabha is also known as the House of the People.

• It plays a crucial role in the law-making process in India.

• Vidhan Sabha

• The Vidhan Sabha is the Lower House of the State Legislature in India.

• Members of the Vidhan Sabha are directly elected by the people of the respective states through general elections held every five years.

• The Vidhan Sabha is also known as the Legislative Assembly.

• It is responsible for making laws on matters listed in the State List and Concurrent List in the Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution.

q: Which of the following statements is correct with respect to the political parties in India?
options: A political party symbol is assigned by the President of India.
India has a multi-party system classified as national, state or regional level.
All parties are registered with the Supreme Court of India.
Status of party is accorded by the Parliament.
solution:
The correct answer is India has a multi-party system classified as national, state or regional level..

Key Points

• India follows a multi-party system where multiple political parties can exist and participate in elections.

• Political parties in India are classified into national, state or regional level based on their performance and influence.

• National parties are those that have influence over a larger part of India, while state or regional parties have influence limited to specific states or regions.

• This classification helps in managing the democratic process and ensuring representation at both the national and state levels.

Additional Information

• Election Commission of India (ECI)

• The Election Commission of India is an autonomous constitutional authority responsible for administering election processes in India at both the national and state levels.

• It administers elections to the Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, and State Legislative Assemblies, as well as the offices of the President and Vice President in the country.

• The ECI ensures free and fair elections in India.

• Registration of Political Parties

• Political parties in India are registered with the Election Commission of India under the Representation of the People Act, 1951.

• Registration with the ECI is a precondition for a political party to be recognized as a national or state party.

• Recognition of Political Parties

• The status of a political party, whether national or state, is determined based on its performance in elections.

• Criteria for recognition include the number of seats won in elections and the percentage of votes obtained.

• Symbols of Political Parties

• The Election Commission of India assigns symbols to political parties to help voters identify them during elections.

• Symbols play a significant role in the election process, especially for illiterate voters who may not recognize party names.

q: Which of the following Articles states that the Prime Minister should be appointed by the President?
solution:
The correct answer is Article 75.

Key Points

• Article 75 of the Indian Constitution deals with the appointment of the Prime Minister and other ministers by the President.

• It states that the Prime Minister shall be appointed by the President and the other Ministers shall be appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister.

• The article also discusses the collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers to the House of the People (Lok Sabha).

• It mentions that the Ministers shall hold office during the pleasure of the President.

Additional Information

• Article 62

• Article 62 deals with the time of holding election to fill a vacancy in the office of President and the term of office of the elected person.

• It specifies that an election to fill the vacancy caused by the expiration of the term of office of President shall be completed before the expiration of the term.

• It also states that an election to fill a vacancy in the office of President occurring by reason of his death, resignation, or removal, or otherwise, shall be held as soon as possible after, and in no case later than six months from, the date of occurrence of the vacancy.

• Article 66

• Article 66 deals with the election of the Vice-President of India.

• The Vice-President is elected by the members of an electoral college consisting of the members of both Houses of Parliament.

• The election is held in accordance with the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote and the voting is by secret ballot.

• Article 71

• Article 71 deals with matters relating to, or connected with, the election of a President or Vice-President.

• It states that all doubts and disputes arising out of or in connection with the election of a President or Vice-President shall be inquired into and decided by the Supreme Court whose decision shall be final.

q: Articles 245 to 255 in Part XI of the Indian Constitution deal with the .
options: financial relations between the Centre and the states
legislative relations between the Centre and the states
solution:
The correct answer is legislative relations between the Centre and the states.

Key Points

• Articles 245 to 255 in Part XI of the Indian Constitution deal with the legislative relations between the Centre and the states.

• These provisions outline the distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the State legislatures.

• Article 245 states the extent of laws made by Parliament and by the Legislatures of States.

• Article 246 deals with the subject-matter of laws made by Parliament and by the Legislatures of States, emphasizing the three lists: Union List, State List, and Concurrent List.

Additional Information

• Emergency Provisions (Articles 352 to 360)

• These articles cover the proclamation of emergency by the President of India.

• They include National Emergency (Article 352), President's Rule (Article 356), and Financial Emergency (Article 360).

• Financial Relations (Articles 268 to 293)

• These articles outline the financial relations between the Centre and the States.

• They cover topics such as distribution of revenues, grants-in-aid, and borrowing powers of the Centre and States.

• Tribunals (Articles 323A to 323B)

• These articles provide for the establishment of administrative tribunals for the adjudication or trial of disputes and offenses.

• Article 323A deals with administrative tribunals, while Article 323B deals with tribunals for other matters.

q: Which of the following is the most controversial Article in the Indian Constitution, which provides for President's rule in an state?
solution:
The correct answer is Article 356.

Key Points

• Article 356 of the Indian Constitution deals with the imposition of President's Rule in states.

• This article is also known as the "President's Rule" or "State Emergency."

• It allows the President of India to take over the functions of the state government if the state government is unable to function according to the provisions of the Constitution.

• President's Rule can be imposed for a maximum period of six months at a time and can be extended with the approval of the Parliament, but not beyond three years.

Additional Information

• Article 352

• Article 352 of the Indian Constitution deals with the proclamation of National Emergency.

• It can be declared due to war, external aggression, or armed rebellion.

• During a National Emergency, the central government gains sweeping powers, and the state governments come under the direct control of the central government.

• This can be proclaimed by the President of India based on the written advice of the Cabinet.

• Article 358

• Article 358 provides for the suspension of the rights guaranteed by Article 19 during a National Emergency.

• It states that while a National Emergency is in operation, nothing in Article 19 shall restrict the power of the State to make any law or to take any executive action abridging or taking away the rights conferred by Article 19.

• Article 360

• Article 360 of the Indian Constitution deals with the proclamation of Financial Emergency.

• The President can declare a Financial Emergency if the financial stability or credit of India or any part of its territory is threatened.

• During a Financial Emergency, the executive authority of the Union extends to giving directions to any state to observe such canons of financial propriety as may be specified in the directions.

• However, no Financial Emergency has been declared in India so far.

q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution mentions that ‘The State shall endeavour to promote cottage industries on an individual or co-operative basis in rural areas’?
solution:
The correct answer is Article 43.

Key Points

• Article 43 of the Indian Constitution is part of the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP).

• It states that 'The State shall endeavour to promote cottage industries on an individual or co-operative basis in rural areas'.

• The objective of this article is to promote economic growth and self-sufficiency in rural areas.

• It aims to provide economic opportunities and employment in rural areas through the promotion of small-scale industries.

Additional Information

• Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)

• The DPSP are guidelines or principles given to the federal institutes governing the state of India, to be kept in consideration while framing laws and policies.

• They are enshrined in Part IV (Articles 36-51) of the Indian Constitution.

• These principles are aimed at ensuring social and economic democracy through a welfare state.

• While they are non-justiciable, meaning they are not legally enforceable by the courts for their violation, they are considered fundamental in the governance of the country.

• Cottage Industries

• Cottage industries are small-scale, decentralized manufacturing businesses often operated out of a home rather than a purpose-built facility.

• They typically involve the production of handmade goods and are labor-intensive.

• These industries play a vital role in the economy by providing employment and promoting traditional crafts.

• In rural areas, cottage industries help in reducing unemployment and migration to urban areas by providing local employment opportunities.

• Rural Development

• Rural development involves improving the quality of life and economic well-being of people living in rural areas, often relatively isolated and sparsely populated areas.

• It focuses on the development of infrastructure, education, healthcare, and employment opportunities.

• Promoting cottage industries is one way to achieve rural development by utilizing local resources and skills.

• Government policies and programs often aim to support rural development through various schemes and initiatives.

q: Which of the following is NOT a Fundamental Duty?
options: To prohibit trade in rare and endangered species
To value and preserve rich heritage of the country's composite culture
To safeguard public property and to abjure violence
To uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India
solution:
The correct answer is To prohibit trade in rare and endangered species.

Key Points

• Fundamental Duties are a set of moral obligations enshrined in Part IVA of the Indian Constitution.

• These duties were added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, upon the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee.

• They aim to promote a spirit of patriotism and uphold the unity of India.

• While the fundamental duties do not include "To prohibit trade in rare and endangered species," they do consist of duties like respecting the national flag, cherishing the heritage, and protecting the environment.

Additional Information

• Fundamental Duties

• Fundamental Duties are outlined in Article 51A of the Indian Constitution.

• There are currently 11 Fundamental Duties listed for the citizens of India.

• Some of the key duties include respecting the Constitution, promoting harmony, protecting the environment, and developing a scientific temper.

• These duties act as a reminder to citizens that while they enjoy their rights, they also have responsibilities towards the nation.

• 42nd Amendment Act, 1976

• Often referred to as the "Mini-Constitution" due to its wide-ranging impact on the Indian Constitution.

• It was enacted during the Emergency period under Prime Minister Indira Gandhi's government.

• In addition to introducing the Fundamental Duties, it also added the words "Socialist," "Secular," and "Integrity" to the Preamble.

• The amendment brought significant changes to the Constitution, including the extension of the duration of legislatures, administrative reforms, and judicial reforms.

• Swaran Singh Committee

• Formed in 1976 to make recommendations on constitutional amendments.

• The committee was headed by Swaran Singh, a senior Congress leader and former Union Minister.

• Its primary recommendations included the inclusion of Fundamental Duties and strengthening the Centre's power.

• The committee's recommendations laid the groundwork for the 42nd Amendment Act.

• Environment Protection

• While the Fundamental Duties do not explicitly mention prohibiting trade in rare and endangered species, they do emphasize the protection and improvement of the natural environment, including forests, lakes, rivers, and wildlife.

• Citizens are encouraged to develop a sense of environmental responsibility and contribute to the preservation of biodiversity.

• Various laws and policies, such as the Wildlife Protection Act, are in place to regulate and prohibit such trade.

• These efforts are crucial for maintaining ecological balance and safeguarding the country's natural heritage.

q: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution CANNOT be suspended even during an emergency declared on the grounds of war or external aggression?
solution:
The correct answer is Articles 20 and 21.

Key Points

• Article 20 of the Indian Constitution deals with the protection of certain rights in the case of conviction for offenses. It prohibits ex-post-facto laws, double jeopardy, and self-incrimination.

• Article 21 guarantees the right to life and personal liberty. It states that no person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to the procedure established by law.

• Both Articles 20 and 21 are fundamental rights under Part III of the Indian Constitution and remain enforceable during times of emergency.

• Under Article 359 of the Constitution, the President can suspend the right to move any court for the enforcement of other fundamental rights during an emergency, but Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended.

Additional Information

• Article 15 and 17:

• Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth.

• Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form.

• These articles can be suspended during an emergency.

• Article 14 and 16:

• Article 14 ensures equality before the law and equal protection of the laws within India.

• Article 16 guarantees equality of opportunity in matters of public employment.

• These articles can also be suspended during an emergency.

• Article 30 and 32:

• Article 30 provides rights of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions.

• Article 32 provides the right to constitutional remedies for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.

• These articles can also be suspended during an emergency.

q: In which of the following years was the Right of Persons with Disabilities Act passed?
solution:
The correct answer is 2016.

Key Points

• The Right of Persons with Disabilities Act was passed in the year 2016.

• This act replaced the earlier Persons with Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection of Rights, and Full Participation) Act, 1995.

• The act aims to give effect to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, which India ratified in 2007.

• The act covers a range of rights and entitlements for persons with disabilities, including education, employment, and social security.

Additional Information

• Persons with Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection of Rights, and Full Participation) Act, 1995

• This was the first comprehensive law in India concerning the rights of persons with disabilities.

• It provided for equal opportunities and full participation of persons with disabilities in society.

• The act focused on prevention and early detection of disabilities, education, employment, and non-discrimination.

• United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD)

• The UNCRPD is an international human rights treaty aimed at protecting the rights and dignity of persons with disabilities.

• Adopted on 13 December 2006 and entered into force on 3 May 2008.

• India signed the convention on 30 March 2007 and ratified it on 1 October 2007.

• The convention requires countries to promote, protect, and ensure the full and equal enjoyment of all human rights by persons with disabilities.

• Right of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016

• This act was enacted to comply with the UNCRPD and to address the gaps in the 1995 Act.

• It recognizes 21 types of disabilities, compared to 7 in the 1995 Act.

• The act mandates that persons with disabilities have the right to equality, life with dignity, and respect for their integrity.

• It includes provisions for reservation in education and employment, social security, and accessibility.

q: The oath of office to the Vice-President is administered by the .
solution:
The correct answer is President.

Key Points

• The oath of office to the Vice-President of India is administered by the President of India.

• This ceremony usually takes place in the Central Hall of Parliament.

• The Vice-President, before entering upon his office, makes and subscribes to an oath or affirmation.

• In the oath, the Vice-President swears to bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution of India and to discharge the duties of his office faithfully.

Additional Information

• Chief Justice of India:

• The Chief Justice of India (CJI) is the head of the judiciary of India and the Supreme Court of India.

• The CJI is responsible for the allocation of cases and appointment of constitutional benches that deal with important matters of law.

• They hold the position until they reach the age of 65.

• Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG):

• The CAG is an authority, established by the Constitution of India, who audits all receipts and expenditure of the Government of India and the state governments.

• The CAG is also the external auditor of government-owned corporations and conducts supplementary audits of government companies.

• The CAG is appointed for a term of six years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier.

• Prime Minister:

• The Prime Minister of India is the head of government and is appointed by the President of India.

• The Prime Minister leads the executive branch of the Government of India and is the chief advisor to the President of India.

• The Prime Minister is usually the leader of the party or coalition that has a majority in the Lok Sabha.

q: Which of the following commissions/committees identified the existence of legal provisions for implementation of some of the Fundamental Duties?
solution:
The correct answer is Justice Verma Committee.

Key Points

• The Justice Verma Committee was established to recommend amendments to criminal laws to provide for quicker trial and enhanced punishment for criminals accused of committing sexual assault against women.

• One of the significant contributions of the Justice Verma Committee was identifying the existence of legal provisions for the implementation of some of the Fundamental Duties.

• The Committee underscored the importance of fundamental duties as a counterpart to fundamental rights, emphasizing their role in ensuring the proper functioning of democracy.

• The recommendations of the Justice Verma Committee have been instrumental in shaping reforms in India's legal framework, especially concerning women's safety and legal provisions related to fundamental duties.

Additional Information

• Fundamental Duties:

• Fundamental Duties are specified in Part IV-A of the Indian Constitution (Article 51A).

• They were added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, upon the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee.

• Originally, ten duties were listed; the 86th Amendment Act, 2002, added an eleventh duty.

• These duties are moral obligations on all citizens to help promote a spirit of patriotism and to uphold the unity of India.

• Justice Verma Committee:

• The Justice Verma Committee was constituted in the wake of the 2012 Delhi gang-rape case.

• It was tasked with reviewing existing laws and suggesting changes to ensure the safety and dignity of women.

• Its report, submitted in January 2013, made several landmark recommendations for legal reforms.

• The Committee's work led to the enactment of the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013, which introduced stricter penalties for sexual crimes.

• Sarkaria Commission:

• Formed in 1983, the Sarkaria Commission was set up to review the working of the Indian federal system and the balance of power between the state and central governments.

• It submitted its report in 1988 with recommendations to improve center-state relations.

• Rajamannar Commission:

• The Rajamannar Committee, established by the Tamil Nadu government in 1969, was tasked with examining center-state relations.

• It recommended greater autonomy for states and the establishment of a permanent inter-state council.

q: Directive principles of State Policy were added to the Indian Constitution by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1976.
solution:
The correct answer is Four

Key Points

Four Directive Principles of State Policy were added to the Indian Constitution by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1976.

• Article 39A – Equal justice and free legal aid.

• Article 43A – Participation of workers in the management of industries.

• Article 48A – Protection and improvement of the environment and safeguarding of forests and wildlife.

• Article 39(f) – Protection of children and youth from exploitation and moral and material abandonment (added to modify Article 39).

Additional Information

• Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)

• The Directive Principles of State Policy are guidelines or principles given to the federal institutes governing the state of India, to be kept in consideration while framing laws and policies.

• They are enumerated in Part IV of the Constitution from Articles 36 to 51.

• The principles aim to create social and economic conditions under which the citizens can lead a good life.

• They are non-justiciable in nature, meaning they are not enforceable by any court, but the principles laid down are considered fundamental in the governance of the country.

• 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976

• Also known as the "Mini-Constitution", this amendment brought about significant changes to the Indian Constitution.

• It attempted to reduce the powers of the Supreme Court and High Courts and gave Parliament unlimited power to amend the Constitution, among other changes.

• It also added ten Fundamental Duties to the Constitution.

• Many of its provisions were later repealed by the 44th Amendment Act of 1978.

q: Which Article in the fundamental duty is invoked when you see in a private party that the Indian flag has been used as a covering for the speaker's desk?
solution:
The correct answer is Article 51A (a).

Key Points

• Article 51A (a) of the Indian Constitution lays down the fundamental duty of every citizen to respect the national symbols, including the National Flag.

• It states that it is the duty of every citizen of India "to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem".

• The use of the Indian Flag as a covering for a speaker's desk at a private party is a violation of this fundamental duty.

• Respecting the National Flag is a manifestation of respect for the nation itself and its values and ideals.

Additional Information

• Fundamental Duties

• The Fundamental Duties are a set of moral obligations enumerated in Part IVA (Article 51A) of the Indian Constitution.

• They were added by the 42nd Amendment Act in 1976 upon the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee.

• Initially, there were ten duties, but an eleventh duty was added by the 86th Amendment in 2002.

• These duties are intended to serve as a constant reminder to every citizen that while enjoying their rights, they have to be conscious of their duties towards the nation.

• National Flag Code of India

• The Flag Code of India, 2002, brings together all laws, conventions, practices, and instructions for the display of the National Flag.

• It governs the usage, hoisting, and display of the Indian Flag to ensure respect and dignity towards the national symbol.

• As per the code, the flag cannot be used for decoration or as a covering in any form.

• Violations of the Flag Code can result in legal consequences under the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971.

• Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971

• This Act prohibits any form of disrespect or insult to the Indian National Flag, the Constitution, the National Anthem, and the National Symbols.

• Disrespect includes acts such as burning, mutilating, defacing, or showing any contempt towards the flag or national symbols.

• Offenders can face imprisonment up to three years, or a fine, or both.

q: Which part of the Constitution deals with the Panchayats?
solution:
The correct answer is Part IX.

Key Points

• Part IX of the Indian Constitution is titled "The Panchayats" and covers Articles 243 to 243O.

• It was introduced by the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1992.

• This part provides a detailed framework for the creation, structure, and functioning of Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) in India.

• It aims to promote decentralized governance and ensure people's participation in rural development.

Additional Information

• 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1992

• This amendment added Part IX and the Eleventh Schedule to the Indian Constitution, effective from April 24, 1993.

• It mandates the establishment of a three-tier system of Panchayati Raj for all states having a population of over 20 lakhs.

• The three tiers are: Gram Panchayat at the village level, Mandal Parishad or Block Samiti at the intermediate level, and Zilla Parishad at the district level.

• The Act also provides for the reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and women.

• Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs)

• PRIs are institutions of rural local governance in India.
