• They are responsible for the administration of rural areas and are involved in the implementation of various developmental programs.

• The structure, functions, and powers of PRIs are defined by the state legislatures in accordance with the Constitutional provisions.

• Decentralized Governance

• Decentralized governance refers to the distribution of power and decision-making authority to lower levels of government, closer to the people.

• It aims to make governance more responsive, accountable, and inclusive.

• In the context of PRIs, it means empowering local bodies to make decisions about local development and administration.

q: Which of the following is mentioned in Article 1 of the Indian constitution?
options: India that is Bharat as federation of states
India that is Bharat as parliamentary democracy
India that is Bharat shall be a Union of states
India that is Bharat as presidential form of democracy
solution:
The correct answer is India that is Bharat shall be a Union of states.

Key Points

• Article 1 of the Indian Constitution states that "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States."

• This signifies that India is a single entity with a union of states rather than a federation of states.

• The term "Union of States" implies that states have no right to secede from the union.

• It defines India as a sovereign, socialist, secular, and democratic republic.

Additional Information

• Union of States

• The phrase "Union of States" was chosen to indicate that the Indian union is not a result of an agreement among the states like the American federation.

• It emphasizes the indestructible nature of the Indian Union, where states cannot secede from the union.

• Sovereign

• The term "sovereign" means that India is independent and free from any external control.

• It has the power to legislate on all matters, both internal and external.

• Socialist

• Although the word "socialist" was added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment Act of 1976, it reflects the commitment to social and economic justice.

• It aims to reduce income inequality and ensure a fair distribution of wealth.

• Secular

• The term "secular" was also added by the 42nd Amendment Act of 1976.

• It means that the state does not have an official religion and treats all religions equally.

• Democratic Republic

• "Democratic" indicates that the government is elected by the people, and "Republic" means that the head of the state is elected and not a hereditary monarch.

• India is committed to the democratic principles of liberty, equality, and fraternity.

q: Articles 52 to 78 in Part V of the Indian Constitution deal with .
solution:
The correct answer is Union Executive.

Key Points

• Articles 52 to 78 in Part V of the Indian Constitution deal with the Union Executive.

• The Union Executive consists of the President, the Vice-President, the Prime Minister, the Council of Ministers, and the Attorney General of India.

• The President of India is the head of the Union Executive and acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister.

• Articles 52 to 62 deal with the President, Articles 63 to 71 deal with the Vice-President, Articles 74 and 75 deal with the Council of Ministers, and Articles 76 and 78 deal with the Attorney General of India and the duties of the Prime Minister.

Additional Information

• Finance Commission of India

• The Finance Commission is a constitutional body for the purpose of allocation of certain revenue resources between the Union and the State Governments.

• It was established under Article 280 of the Indian Constitution.

• The Finance Commission is appointed every five years and consists of a chairman and four other members.

• Amendment of the Constitution

• The procedure for the amendment of the Constitution is laid down in Article 368 in Part XX of the Constitution.

• It provides for a flexible procedure for the amendment to address the changing needs and circumstances of the country.

• An amendment can be initiated only by the introduction of a Bill in either House of Parliament and must be passed by a special majority.

• National Emergency

• National emergency provisions are contained in Article 352 of the Indian Constitution.

• A National Emergency can be declared on the grounds of war, external aggression, or armed rebellion.

• During a National Emergency, the federal structure of the country changes to a unitary one, and the central government becomes more powerful.

q: Articles 214 to 231 in Part VI of the Indian Constitution deal with the .
solution:
The correct answer is High Courts.

Key Points

• Articles 214 to 231 in Part VI of the Indian Constitution deal with the establishment and constitution of the High Courts.

• A High Court is the principal civil court of original jurisdiction in a state.

• Each state of India is provided with a High Court which has its own jurisdiction and powers as defined under the Constitution.

• The High Courts have the authority to issue writs for the enforcement of the Fundamental Rights of citizens.

Additional Information

• High Courts

• High Courts are the highest courts in a state in India, and each state has its own High Court.

• High Courts have jurisdiction over all subordinate courts within their territory.

• They have the power to hear appeals and to issue writs to enforce Fundamental Rights.

• The judges of the High Courts are appointed by the President of India.

• District Courts

• District Courts are established by the state governments of India for every district or for one or more districts together taking into account the number of cases and population distribution.

• They administer justice at the district level and are subordinate to the High Court of the respective state.

• Subordinate Courts

• Subordinate Courts are the lower courts under the District Courts, which deal with civil, criminal, and other cases at a more local level.

• They operate under the supervision and control of the District Court.

• Supreme Court

• The Supreme Court of India is the highest judicial forum and final court of appeal as established by Part V, Chapter IV of the Constitution of India.

• It comprises the Chief Justice of India and a number of other judges appointed by the President of India.

• The Supreme Court has extensive original, appellate, and advisory jurisdictions.

q: The number of ministers, including the Chief Minister, in a state shall NOT be less than _.
solution:
The correct answer is 12.

Key Points

• The number of ministers, including the Chief Minister, in a state shall not be less than 12.

• This provision is part of the 91st Amendment Act of 2003 to the Constitution of India.

• The Amendment was introduced to avoid jumbo ministries and ensure efficient governance.

• The maximum number of ministers in a state, including the Chief Minister, shall not exceed 15% of the total number of members of the Legislative Assembly of that state.

Additional Information

• 91st Amendment Act of 2003

• The 91st Amendment Act was enacted to curb defections and to limit the size of the Council of Ministers to prevent the formation of oversized cabinets.

• It is one of the key measures to ensure stability in the legislative assembly by preventing political horse-trading and defection.

• The Amendment mandates that a person who is disqualified under the Tenth Schedule (anti-defection law) from being a member of the legislature shall also be disqualified from being appointed as a minister or holding any remunerative political post.

• This amendment also ensures that the total number of ministers, including the Prime Minister in the Central Government, shall not exceed 15% of the total number of members of the Parliament in the Lok Sabha.

• Anti-Defection Law (Tenth Schedule)

• The anti-defection law was introduced by the 52nd Amendment Act of 1985 and later strengthened by the 91st Amendment Act of 2003.

• The main objective of the law is to combat the evil of political defections by elected members.

• According to this law, if a member of a house belonging to a political party voluntarily gives up the membership of his party or votes (or abstains from voting) contrary to the directions issued by his party, he can be disqualified from being a member of the house.

• The decision on disqualification questions on the ground of defection is referred to the Chairman or the Speaker of such House and their decision is final.

q: Which of the following Constitution Amendment Bills is related to the provision of modifying the list of Scheduled Caste in Tamil Nadu?
options: The Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order Amendment Act, 2013
solution:
The correct answer is The Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order (Amendment) Bill, 2021.

Key Points

• The Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order (Amendment) Bill, 2021, was introduced to modify the list of Scheduled Castes in Tamil Nadu.

• This amendment bill aims to include certain communities in the list of Scheduled Castes in Tamil Nadu, thereby enabling them to avail benefits and protections guaranteed under the Constitution.

• The bill was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on February 8, 2021, by the Minister of Social Justice and Empowerment.

• Such amendments are periodically made to address the demands and needs of various communities to ensure equitable development and social justice.

Additional Information

• Scheduled Castes

• Scheduled Castes (SCs) are specific groups of people who are historically disadvantaged and have been subjected to untouchability and social exclusion.

• The Constitution of India provides various safeguards to protect and promote the socio-economic interests of SCs, including reservation in education and employment.

• The President of India, in consultation with the Governor of a state, issues orders specifying the SCs in that state.

• From time to time, amendments are made to the list of SCs to include or exclude communities based on social, educational, and economic criteria.

• Constitution Amendment Bills

• Constitution Amendment Bills are proposed changes to the Constitution of India.

• Such bills can be introduced in either house of Parliament and require a two-thirds majority of the members present and voting for passage.

• Amendments to the Constitution address various issues, including the rights of marginalized communities, electoral reforms, and changes in the structure of government.

• The Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order (Amendment) Bill is one such amendment aimed at updating the list of SCs.

• Rajya Sabha

• Rajya Sabha, or the Council of States, is the upper house of India's Parliament.

• Members of the Rajya Sabha are elected by the elected members of State Legislative Assemblies, and by the members of the Electoral college for Union Territories, using a single transferable vote system.

• The Rajya Sabha has a maximum membership of 250 members, of which 12 are nominated by the President of India.

• The Rajya Sabha plays a crucial role in the legislative process, including the passage of amendment bills.

q: Which fundamental duty applies to you when you see your college friends start fighting with the canteen person when he passed a few anti-religious statements?
options: To promote harmony and spirit of brotherhood
To value and preserve the rich heritage
To develop the scientific temper, humanism, and the spirit of inquiry
To protect and improve our natural environment
solution:
The correct answer is To promote harmony and spirit of brotherhood.

Key Points

• The fundamental duty to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood amongst all the people of India transcending religious, linguistic, regional, or sectional diversities is crucial in maintaining unity in diversity.

• This duty highlights the importance of respecting and tolerating different beliefs and practices within the country.

• It encourages citizens to rise above narrow considerations of caste, creed, and religion and to work towards the welfare of society as a whole.

• Promoting harmony and brotherhood is essential for fostering an environment where different communities can coexist peacefully and contribute to national development.

Additional Information

• Fundamental Duties:

• Fundamental Duties are a set of moral obligations that all citizens are expected to follow and respect.

• These duties were added to the Indian Constitution by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, under Article 51A.

• Initially, there were ten fundamental duties, and later, an eleventh duty was added by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002.

• Although these duties are non-justiciable, meaning they are not legally enforceable, they serve as a constant reminder of the responsibilities that come with citizenship.

• Promoting Harmony and Brotherhood:

• This duty is essential in a multicultural and pluralistic society like India, where people from various backgrounds coexist.

• It emphasizes the need for mutual respect, tolerance, and understanding among different communities.

• By promoting harmony, citizens can help prevent conflicts and ensure a peaceful and cohesive society.

• This duty also underscores the importance of national integration and unity, which are vital for the country's progress and development.

• Respect for Diversity:

• India is known for its rich cultural, religious, and linguistic diversity.

• Respecting this diversity is crucial for maintaining social harmony and fostering a sense of belonging among all citizens.

• Encouraging dialogue and interaction between different communities can help bridge gaps and build stronger relationships.

• Diversity should be seen as a strength and a source of inspiration for collective growth and development.

q: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT regarding Fundamental Rights?
options: Fundamental Rights can be enforced by Law.
Fundamental rights are derived from the Britain Constitution.
The Fundamental Rights are mentioned in constitution from article 12 to 35.
solution:
The correct answer is Fundamental rights are derived from the Britain Constitution..

Key Points

• Fundamental Rights are enshrined in Part III of the Indian Constitution, from Article 12 to 35.

• These rights are essential for the overall development of individuals and the preservation of human dignity.

• Article 21 of the Indian Constitution guarantees the Right to Life and Personal Liberty.

• Fundamental Rights are justiciable, meaning they can be enforced through the courts of law in India.

Additional Information

• Fundamental Rights

• Fundamental Rights are the basic human rights guaranteed to all individuals by the Constitution of India. These rights are crucial for the protection and development of individuals.

• They are meant to promote the ideal of political democracy and prevent the arbitrary use of power by the state.

• Some of the key Fundamental Rights include the Right to Equality (Articles 14-18), Right to Freedom (Articles 19-22), Right against Exploitation (Articles 23-24), Right to Freedom of Religion (Articles 25-28), Cultural and Educational Rights (Articles 29-30), and the Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32).

• These rights are enforceable by the courts, and individuals can approach the judiciary to seek protection and enforcement of their Fundamental Rights.

• Enforcement of Fundamental Rights

• Fundamental Rights are justiciable, meaning individuals can approach the courts to enforce these rights if they are violated.

• The Supreme Court and High Courts have the power to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.

• Writs such as habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, and certiorari are used to enforce these rights.

• Right to Life (Article 21)

• Article 21 of the Indian Constitution guarantees the Right to Life and Personal Liberty.

• This article ensures that no person shall be deprived of their life or personal liberty except according to the procedure established by law.

• The Right to Life under Article 21 has been interpreted by the Supreme Court to include various rights such as the right to live with human dignity, right to livelihood, right to health, right to education, and more.

q: Which Article mentions the Comptroller and Auditor General of India?
solution:
The correct answer is Article 148.

Key Points

• Article 148 of the Indian Constitution deals with the appointment, duties, and powers of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG).

• The CAG is responsible for auditing the accounts of the Union and State governments and public sector organizations, ensuring accountability and transparency.

• The CAG is appointed by the President of India and can only be removed from office in a manner similar to the removal of a Supreme Court judge.

• The CAG submits audit reports to the President or the Governor, who then places them before the Parliament or the State Legislature.

Additional Information

• Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG)

• The CAG is the head of the Indian Audit and Accounts Department and acts as the guardian of the public purse.

• The office of the CAG is a constitutional body established under Article 148 of the Constitution of India.

• The CAG audits all receipts and expenditure of the Government of India and the state governments, including those of bodies and authorities substantially financed by the government.

• The CAG ensures that the financial administration of the country is carried out in accordance with the Constitution and the laws made by the Parliament and State Legislatures.

• Article 154

• Article 154 of the Indian Constitution vests the executive power of the State in the Governor.

• It states that the executive power shall be exercised by the Governor either directly or through officers subordinate to him in accordance with the Constitution.

• Article 156

• Article 156 of the Indian Constitution deals with the term of office of the Governor.

• It states that the Governor shall hold office during the pleasure of the President and for a term of five years.

• Article 136

• Article 136 of the Indian Constitution grants special leave to appeal by the Supreme Court.

• It gives the Supreme Court the discretionary power to grant special leave to appeal against any judgment, decree, determination, sentence, or order passed by any court or tribunal in the territory of India.

q: Which Article deals with the election of the President?
solution:
The correct answer is Article 54.

Key Points

• Article 54 of the Indian Constitution deals with the election of the President of India.

• The President is elected by an electoral college consisting of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of States and Union territories.

• The process of election is conducted by the Election Commission of India.

• The election is held in accordance with the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote.

Additional Information

• Article 72:

• Article 72 of the Indian Constitution empowers the President to grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions of punishment or to suspend, remit or commute the sentence of any person convicted of any offense.

• This power can be exercised in all cases where the punishment or sentence is by a court-martial, in cases where the punishment or sentence is for an offense against any law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the Union extends, and in all cases where the sentence is a sentence of death.

• Article 54:

• Article 54 deals with the election of the President.

• The President is elected by an electoral college consisting of elected members of both Houses of Parliament and Legislative Assemblies of States and Union territories.

• The election is held in accordance with the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote.

• Article 74:

• Article 74 of the Indian Constitution states that there shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President.

• The President shall, in the exercise of his functions, act in accordance with such advice.

• Article 66:

• Article 66 deals with the election of the Vice-President of India.

• The Vice-President is elected by the members of an electoral college consisting of the members of both Houses of Parliament.

• The election is held in accordance with the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote.

q: Who is considered the highest law officer of the state in India?
solution:
The correct answer is Advocate General.

Key Points

• The Advocate General of the state is the highest law officer in the state.

• He/she is appointed by the Governor of the state.

• The Advocate General's duty is to advise the state government on legal matters.

• The Advocate General has the right to speak and take part in the proceedings of both houses of the state legislature, but without the right to vote.

Additional Information

• Attorney General of India

• The Attorney General is the highest law officer in the country.

• He/she is appointed by the President of India.

• The Attorney General's duty is to give advice to the Government of India on legal matters and perform other legal duties assigned to him/her.

• The Attorney General has the right to participate in the proceedings of both houses of Parliament but without the right to vote.

• Chief Justice of High Court

• The Chief Justice is the head of the judiciary in a state.

• He/she is appointed by the President of India in consultation with the Chief Justice of India and the Governor of the state.

• The Chief Justice's duty is to preside over the high court and ensure the administration of justice in the state.

• Auditor General

• The Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG) is the authority responsible for auditing the accounts of the state and central governments and public sector organizations.

• The CAG is appointed by the President of India.

• The CAG's duty is to ensure that public funds are used efficiently and for the intended purposes.

q: Which of the following articles of the Indian constitution deals with the parliament and it's proceedings?
solution:
The correct answer is Article 79 to 122.

Key Points

• Article 79 to 122 of the Indian Constitution deals with the Parliament of India and its proceedings.

• These articles cover various aspects such as the composition of Parliament, the powers, and functions of its members, and the procedures for conducting parliamentary business.

• Article 79 establishes a bicameral legislature at the federal level, consisting of the President and two Houses: the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) and the House of the People (Lok Sabha).

• Articles 85 to 122 provide detailed provisions regarding the functioning of Parliament, including sessions, prorogation, dissolution, the conduct of business, and the powers and privileges of its members.

Additional Information

• Article 51A

• Article 51A specifies the fundamental duties of every citizen of India.

• It was added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.

• These duties include respecting the Constitution, promoting harmony, and safeguarding public property, among others.

• Article 36 to 51

• These articles pertain to the Directive Principles of State Policy.

• They provide guidelines to the central and state governments for making policies aimed at establishing a just society.

• Article 12 to 35

• These articles cover the Fundamental Rights guaranteed to the citizens of India.

• They include rights like the right to equality, right to freedom, right against exploitation, right to freedom of religion, cultural and educational rights, and the right to constitutional remedies.

q: Which Committee identified the existence of legal provisions for implementation of some of the Fundamental Duties?
solution:
The correct answer is Justice Verma Committee.

Key Points

• The Justice Verma Committee was formed to identify the existence of legal provisions for the implementation of some of the Fundamental Duties enshrined in the Constitution of India.

• The Committee was set up in 1999 under the chairmanship of Justice J.S. Verma, former Chief Justice of India.

• It reviewed the existing legal framework and suggested measures to make the Fundamental Duties more enforceable.

• The Committee's recommendations emphasized the role of education and awareness in promoting a sense of duty among citizens.

Additional Information

• Fundamental Duties

• The Fundamental Duties are a set of moral obligations for all citizens of India, enshrined in Part IV-A of the Constitution (Article 51A).

• These duties were added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, based on the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee.

• There are currently 11 Fundamental Duties, which include respect for the Constitution, national symbols, the promotion of harmony, and the protection of public property.

• The Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable, meaning they are not legally enforceable by the courts.

• Justice Verma Committee

• Justice J.S. Verma, a renowned jurist and former Chief Justice of India, chaired the committee.

• The Committee's focus was to enhance the implementation of Fundamental Duties through legal and educational reforms.

• It highlighted the need for incorporating the Fundamental Duties into the education system to instill a sense of responsibility in citizens from a young age.

• The Committee's report has been influential in shaping policies and programs aimed at promoting civic responsibility.

• 42nd Amendment Act, 1976

• The 42nd Amendment Act is also known as the "Mini-Constitution" due to its extensive changes to the Constitution of India.

• It introduced the Fundamental Duties, provided for the establishment of Administrative Tribunals, and made several changes to the Preamble and other parts of the Constitution.

• The Amendment was passed during the Emergency period under Prime Minister Indira Gandhi's government.

• It aimed to strengthen the central government's powers and bring about socio-economic reforms.

q: Which of the following Constitutional Amendment Acts led to formation of the Goods and Services Tax Council?
solution:
The correct answer is 101st Constitutional Amendment Act.

Key Points

• The 101st Constitutional Amendment Act was passed by the Indian Parliament in August 2016.

• This amendment led to the introduction of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) in India, which came into effect on 1st July 2017.

• The GST Council was formed as per Article 279A of the Indian Constitution, inserted by the 101st Amendment.

• The GST Council is responsible for making recommendations on the rates of taxes, goods and services that may be subjected or exempted from GST, and other related matters.

Additional Information

• 102nd Constitutional Amendment Act

• This amendment came into effect in 2018.

• It granted constitutional status to the National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC).

• Article 338B was inserted to provide for the NCBC.

• 100th Constitutional Amendment Act

• This amendment was passed in 2015.

• It dealt with the exchange of certain enclaves between India and Bangladesh and the demarcation of the boundary between the two countries.

• It facilitated the implementation of the Land Boundary Agreement (LBA) between India and Bangladesh.

• 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act

• This amendment came into effect in 2019.

• It introduced a 10% reservation for economically weaker sections (EWS) in government jobs and educational institutions.

• Articles 15(6) and 16(6) were added to the Constitution to enable this reservation.

• Goods and Services Tax (GST)

• GST is a comprehensive, multi-stage, destination-based tax that is levied on every value addition.

• It replaced multiple indirect taxes previously levied by the central and state governments.

• GST is categorized into Central GST (CGST), State GST (SGST), Integrated GST (IGST), and Union Territory GST (UTGST).

• The GST Council, chaired by the Union Finance Minister, is a federal body where both the center and the states participate in the decision-making process.

q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution provides for protecting and improving the environment and safeguarding forests and wildlife?
solution:
The correct answer is Article 48-A.

Key Points

• Article 48-A of the Indian Constitution specifically deals with the Protection and improvement of the environment and safeguarding of forests and wildlife.
• It falls under Part IV of the Indian Constitution, which encompasses the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP).
• This article was added to the Constitution by the 42nd Amendment Act of 1976.
• According to Article 48-A, the State shall endeavor to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wildlife of the country.
Additional Information

• Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)
• These are guidelines or principles given to the central and state governments of India, to be kept in mind while framing laws and policies.
• They are non-justiciable, meaning their application cannot be enforced by the courts.
• However, they are considered fundamental in the governance of the country, aiming to create social and economic conditions under which citizens can lead a good life.
• 42nd Amendment Act of 1976
• This amendment is also known as the "Mini-Constitution" due to the significant changes it brought to the Indian Constitution.
• It added new directives in the form of Article 48-A and Article 51-A(g) which deals with the protection of the environment and the duty of citizens to protect the environment, respectively.
• It also added ten fundamental duties to the Constitution, emphasizing the responsibility of citizens towards the nation.
• Environmental Protection
• It refers to the practice of protecting the natural environment by individuals, organizations, and governments.
• The primary goal is to conserve natural resources and the existing natural environment and, where possible, to repair damage and reverse trends.
• In India, various laws and regulations have been implemented to ensure environmental protection, including the Environment Protection Act of 1986.
• Forest and Wildlife Conservation
• Conservation of forests and wildlife is crucial for maintaining the ecological balance and biodiversity.
• In India, this is governed by various laws, including the Indian Forest Act, 1927, and the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972.
• These laws aim to regulate and manage forest resources and protect wildlife species from exploitation and extinction.

q: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution mentions that 'The State shall, in particular, direct its policy towards securing that the ownership and control of the material resources of the community are so distributed as best to subserve the common good'?
solution:
The correct answer is Article 39(b).

Key Points

• Article 39(b) is a part of the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) in the Indian Constitution.

• It emphasizes that the ownership and control of the material resources of the community should be distributed in a manner that best serves the common good.

• This principle aims to reduce economic inequalities and ensure equitable distribution of resources.

• Article 39(b) reflects the socialist philosophy embedded in the Indian Constitution, focusing on social justice and economic welfare.

Additional Information

• Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)

• The DPSPs are guidelines for the framing of laws by the government. These principles are considered fundamental in the governance of the country.

• They are not enforceable by any court, but the principles laid down are considered in the governance of the state.

• The aim of the DPSPs is to create social and economic conditions under which citizens can lead a good life.

• They are mentioned in Part IV of the Indian Constitution, from Articles 36 to 51.

• Article 39(a)

• It directs the state to ensure that the citizens, men, and women equally, have the right to an adequate means of livelihood.

• Article 39(c)

• It aims to ensure that the operation of the economic system does not result in the concentration of wealth and means of production to the common detriment.

• Article 39(d)

• It mandates that there is equal pay for equal work for both men and women.

q: If a 12-year-old is found to be working in a factory manufacturing carpets, which of the following Articles of the Constitution of India will be violated?
solution:
The correct answer is Article 24.

Key Points

• Article 24 of the Constitution of India prohibits the employment of children below the age of 14 years in any factory, mine, or other hazardous employment.

• This Article is part of the Fundamental Rights enshrined in Part III of the Constitution, which aims to protect children from exploitation.

• It was introduced to safeguard children from engaging in work that can be detrimental to their health, safety, and development.

• Violation of this Article can lead to legal consequences and penalties as per the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986.

Additional Information

• Article 23:

• Prohibits human trafficking and forced labor.

• It states that traffic in human beings, begar (forced labor), and other similar forms of forced labor are prohibited and any contravention of this provision shall be an offense punishable in accordance with the law.

• Article 25:

• Guarantees freedom of conscience and free profession, practice, and propagation of religion.

• It provides all individuals the right to freely profess, practice, and propagate their religion, subject to public order, morality, and health.

• Article 26:

• Provides freedom to manage religious affairs.

• It gives every religious denomination or any section thereof the right to establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes, manage its own affairs in matters of religion, own and acquire movable and immovable property, and administer such property in accordance with the law.

• Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986:

• This Act prohibits the engagement of children in certain employments and regulates the conditions of work of children in other employments.

• The Act defines a child as a person who has not completed 14 years of age.

• It lays down a detailed framework for the prohibition and regulation of child labor in India.

q: Which of the following states is one of those states that have no Panchayati Raj Institution at all?
solution:
The correct answer is Nagaland.

Key Points

• Nagaland does not have Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) due to its unique traditional and customary laws.

• The Nagaland Village and Area Councils Act, 1978 governs local governance in the state instead of the Panchayati Raj system.

• The Constitution (Seventy-Third Amendment) Act, 1992, which introduced the Panchayati Raj system in India, does not apply to Nagaland.

• Nagaland's traditional village councils and customary practices are protected under Article 371(A) of the Indian Constitution.

Additional Information

• Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs)

• Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) are a system of rural local self-government in India.

• The system was institutionalized through the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992.

• This act provides a three-tier system of Panchayati Raj for all states having a population of over 2 million, consisting of:

• Gram Panchayat at the village level

• Panchayat Samiti at the intermediate level

• Zila Parishad at the district level

• The objective of PRIs is to ensure democracy at the grassroots level and empower rural India.

• Article 371(A)

• Article 371(A) of the Indian Constitution provides special provisions with respect to the state of Nagaland.

• It ensures that no act of Parliament in respect of religious or social practices, Naga customary law and procedure, administration of civil and criminal justice involving decisions according to Naga customary law, ownership and transfer of land and its resources shall apply to Nagaland unless the Legislative Assembly of Nagaland by a resolution so decides.

• This article preserves the unique social and cultural practices of Nagaland.

• Nagaland Village and Area Councils Act, 1978

• This act provides for the establishment of village councils in Nagaland.

• Village councils are responsible for administration, development, and maintaining law and order in villages.

• The members of the village councils are selected according to the traditional customs and practices of the Naga tribes.

• This act ensures that local governance in Nagaland respects and incorporates the traditional and customary laws of the Naga people.

q: When did a States Reorganisation Commission was set up, which recommended the creation of linguistic States on the basis of larger linguistic groups?
solution:
The correct answer is December 1953.

Key Points

• The States Reorganisation Commission (SRC) was formed in December 1953.

• The Commission was tasked with recommending the reorganization of state boundaries based on linguistic lines.

• The SRC was headed by Fazal Ali and its other members were H.N. Kunzru and K.M. Panikkar.

• The recommendations of the SRC led to the passage of the States Reorganisation Act in 1956, which redefined the boundaries of Indian states.

Additional Information

• States Reorganisation Commission (SRC):

• The SRC was constituted by the Government of India in 1953 to address demands for the reorganization of India's states on linguistic lines.

• The SRC's primary objective was to ensure that state boundaries were redrawn to reflect the linguistic and cultural identities of the populations within them.

• The Commission's final report was submitted in 1955, and it recommended the reorganization of states primarily on linguistic lines.

• The recommendations of the SRC were implemented through the States Reorganisation Act of 1956, which led to the creation of 14 states and 6 union territories.

• Fazal Ali:

• Fazal Ali was an Indian civil servant and politician who served as the head of the States Reorganisation Commission.

• He played a crucial role in the reorganization of Indian states based on linguistic lines.

• His leadership and contributions were instrumental in shaping the modern political map of India.

• States Reorganisation Act, 1956:

• The States Reorganisation Act was a major reform of the boundaries and governance structures of Indian states, implemented in 1956.

• This act led to the creation of several new states and union territories, primarily based on linguistic and cultural commonalities.

• It aimed to address the demands for statehood from various linguistic and regional groups within India.

• The Act marked a significant step towards accommodating the diverse linguistic and cultural identities within the Indian union.

q: Which part of the Indian Constitution deals with the Election Commission?
solution:
The correct answer is Part XV.

Key Points

• Part XV of the Indian Constitution deals with elections, which includes provisions related to the Election Commission of India.

• It encompasses Articles 324 to 329, which provide the framework for the conduct of elections in the country.

• Article 324 specifically vests the power of superintendence, direction, and control of elections in an independent Election Commission.

• The Election Commission is responsible for conducting elections to the Parliament, state legislatures, and offices of the President and Vice-President in India.

Additional Information

• Part XII of the Indian Constitution deals with finance, property, contracts, and suits. It includes provisions related to the distribution of revenue between the Union and the States.

• Part IV contains the Directive Principles of State Policy, which are guidelines for the framing of laws by the government. These principles aim to create social and economic conditions under which citizens can lead a good life.

• Part XI deals with the relations between the Union and the States, defining the distribution of legislative and administrative powers between the two.

• The Election Commission of India is an autonomous constitutional authority responsible for administering election processes in India at both national and state levels. The body administers elections to the Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, and State Legislative Assemblies in India, as well as the offices of the President and Vice President in the country.

• Being a constitutional body, the Election Commission operates independently of the government to ensure free and fair elections. Its autonomy and impartial functioning are crucial for the democratic structure of the country.

q: As per article 158, the Governor shall NOT be a member of either House of Parliament or of a House of the Legislature of any State specified in _ Schedule.
solution:
The correct answer is First.

Key Points

• According to Article 158 of the Indian Constitution, the Governor of a State shall not be a member of either House of Parliament or of a House of the Legislature of any State specified in the First Schedule.

• The First Schedule of the Indian Constitution lists the states and union territories of India.

• This provision ensures the independence of the Governor's office from legislative influence.

• The Governor must resign from any legislative positions before assuming office to maintain this separation of powers.

Additional Information

• Article 158

• Article 158 of the Constitution of India pertains to the conditions of the Governor's office.

• Clause (1) of Article 158 states that the Governor shall not be a member of either House of Parliament or of a House of the Legislature of any State specified in the First Schedule.

• This clause ensures that the Governor remains unbiased and can execute his/her duties without any legislative pressures.

• First Schedule

• The First Schedule of the Indian Constitution details the list of States and Union Territories along with their respective territories.

• It provides the official names of the States and Union Territories and their territorial boundaries.

• Role of the Governor

• The Governor is the Constitutional head of a state in India.

• He/she is appointed by the President of India and holds office at the President's pleasure.

• The Governor's role includes giving assent to bills passed by the state legislature, appointing the Chief Minister, and ensuring the state administration is carried out according to the Constitution.

q: The concept of ‘Independence of judiciary’ in the Indian Constitution is taken from the Constitution of:
solution:
The correct answer is The USA.

Key Points

• The concept of 'Independence of judiciary' is a fundamental principle of the United States Constitution.

• In the United States, the judiciary is an independent branch of government, separate from the executive and legislative branches.

• This principle ensures that the judiciary can make decisions free from political pressure or influence.

• The Indian Constitution incorporated this principle to ensure a fair and impartial judicial system.

Additional Information

• Independence of Judiciary

• It refers to the concept that the judiciary should be independent from the other branches of government (executive and legislative).

• It ensures that judges are free to make decisions based on law, without external influence or pressure.

• This principle is crucial for maintaining the rule of law and protecting the rights and liberties of individuals.

• Judiciary in the United States

• The U.S. Constitution establishes the judiciary as a separate and co-equal branch of government.

• The judiciary has the power of judicial review, which allows courts to declare laws or executive actions unconstitutional.

• Federal judges are appointed for life, which helps to secure their independence.

• Judiciary in India

• The Indian Constitution adopts the principle of judicial independence to ensure that the judiciary is free from any external control.

• Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts are appointed by the President of India and can be removed only through a rigorous process of impeachment.

• The judiciary in India has the power of judicial review to ensure that laws and executive actions comply with the Constitution.

q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution mentions about the 'Promotion of educational and economic interests of Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and other weaker sections'?
solution:
The correct answer is Article 46.

Key Points

• Article 46 of the Indian Constitution falls under the Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV).

• It mandates the State to promote the educational and economic interests of Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and other weaker sections of society.

• The article aims at protecting these groups from social injustice and all forms of exploitation.

• It emphasizes the need for providing special care to the educational and economic development of these vulnerable sections.

Additional Information

• Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP):

• These are guidelines or principles given to the federal institutes governing the state of India, to be kept in consideration while framing laws and policies.

• They are non-justiciable in nature, meaning they are not enforceable by the courts for their violation.

• However, they are fundamental in the governance of the country and aim to create social and economic conditions under which the citizens can lead a good life.

• The Directive Principles are inspired by the Irish Constitution and are aimed at ensuring social and economic democracy.

• Scheduled Castes (SCs):

• These are historically disadvantaged groups recognized in the Indian Constitution.

• They are provided with positive discrimination or affirmative action to uplift their status in society.

• Special provisions are made for their representation in various sectors such as education, employment, and legislature.

• Scheduled Tribes (STs):

• These are indigenous communities who are distinct from the mainstream population in terms of culture, language, and social practices.

• Like SCs, STs are also provided with affirmative action to protect their rights and promote their development.

• Efforts are made to preserve their cultural heritage and ensure their socio-economic development.

• Other Weaker Sections:

• This term generally refers to other socially and economically disadvantaged groups that are not classified as SCs or STs.

• Special measures are taken to ensure their upliftment and integration into the mainstream society.

• These measures may include reservations, scholarships, and other welfare schemes.

q: Which of the following are enumerated in Part IV of the Indian Constitution, from Articles 36 to 51?
solution:
The correct answer is Directive Principles of State Policy.

Key Points

• The Directive Principles of State Policy are enumerated in Part IV of the Indian Constitution, from Articles 36 to 51.

• These principles are guidelines for the framing of laws by the government.

• They aim to create social and economic conditions under which citizens can lead a good life.

• Although these principles are non-justiciable, meaning they are not enforceable by any court, they are considered fundamental in the governance of the country.

Additional Information

• Fundamental Rights

• These are a set of rights that are guaranteed to all citizens of India by the Constitution.

• Fundamental Duties

• These are moral obligations that are expected to be followed by all citizens of India.

• They are mentioned in Part IV-A of the Indian Constitution under Article 51A.

• There are 11 Fundamental Duties listed in the Constitution.

• They were added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, based on the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee.

• The Union

• This pertains to the structure and functioning of the Union Government in India.

• It is covered in Part V of the Indian Constitution from Articles 52 to 151.

• It includes provisions related to the President, Vice-President, Council of Ministers, Parliament, and other Union bodies.

q: UPSC is a Constitutional Body to conduct examinations for appointments to the services of the Union and the services of the State, respectively, under Article .
solution:
The correct answer is Article 315.

Key Points

• Article 315 of the Indian Constitution deals with the functions of the Public Service Commissions (both Union and State).

• The Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) is a central recruiting agency in India responsible for appointments to and examinations for All India Services and Group A & B of Central services.

• The State Public Service Commissions (SPSCs) are responsible for conducting examinations for appointments to the services of the respective state governments.

• The duties of the UPSC and SPSCs include conducting examinations for appointments to the services, advising on the suitability of candidates for various posts, and advising on disciplinary matters affecting government employees.

Additional Information

• Union Public Service Commission (UPSC)

• The UPSC is an independent constitutional body established under Article 315 of the Indian Constitution.

• It is tasked with conducting examinations for All India Services, Central Services, and public services of the centrally administered territories.

• The commission consists of a chairman and other members appointed by the President of India.

• The term of office of the members of the Commission is six years or until they attain the age of 65 years, whichever is earlier.

• State Public Service Commissions (SPSCs)

• Each state in India has its own Public Service Commission established under Article 315 to conduct examinations for appointments to the services of the state.

• The SPSCs advise the state government on all matters relating to recruitment, promotions, transfers, and disciplinary actions.

• The members of the SPSC are appointed by the Governor of the respective state.

• The term of office for SPSC members is also six years or until the age of 62 years, whichever is earlier.

q: The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 empowers the  to establish authorities charged with the mandate of preventing environmental pollution in all its forms.
solution:
The correct answer is Central Government.

Key Points

• The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, is an Act of the Parliament of India, enacted in the wake of the Bhopal Gas Tragedy.

• The Act empowers the Central Government to make rules to regulate environmental pollution and to establish authorities for the purpose.

• It provides the Central Government with the authority to take all necessary measures to protect and improve the quality of the environment.

• It encompasses a wide range of regulations and standards to control pollution and manage hazardous substances.

Additional Information

• Environment (Protection) Act, 1986

• The Act was passed in response to the need for overarching legislation to protect and improve the environment.

• The Act gives the Central Government the power to take measures for environmental protection, such as setting standards for emissions or discharge of environmental pollutants from various sources.

• It provides a framework for coordinating the activities of various central and state authorities established under other laws to ensure environmental protection.

• The Act also includes provisions for penalties for contravention of the standards and restrictions set by the government.

• Key Provisions of the Act

• Section 3: Empowers the Central Government to take measures to protect and improve the environment and to prevent, control, and abate environmental pollution.

• Section 6: Empowers the Central Government to make rules to regulate environmental pollution, including standards for the quality of the environment, and the maximum allowable concentrations of various pollutants.

• Section 15: Provides for penalties for non-compliance with the provisions of the Act, including imprisonment and fines.

• Section 19: Allows any person to file a complaint in a court of law against anyone who fails to comply with the Act's provisions.

• Importance of the Act

• The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, serves as a comprehensive framework for the protection and improvement of the environment in India.

• It addresses the need for a unified approach to environmental regulation and management.

• The Act empowers the government to take proactive measures to prevent environmental degradation and to respond effectively to environmental emergencies.

• It plays a crucial role in ensuring sustainable development and safeguarding public health and well-being.

q: Which of the following Articles and Parts of the Indian Constitution deal with the State Legislature?
solution:
The correct answer is Articles 168 to 212 in Part VI.

Key Points

• Articles 168 to 212 in Part VI of the Indian Constitution deal with the State Legislature.

• The State Legislature consists of the Governor and one or two Houses, as the case may be.

• In some states, the legislature is bicameral, consisting of the Legislative Assembly and the Legislative Council, while in others, it is unicameral, consisting only of the Legislative Assembly.

• These articles lay down the composition, duration, and functions of the State Legislatures.

Additional Information

• Article 168: This article specifies the composition of the State Legislature, which can be either unicameral (with only the Legislative Assembly) or bicameral (with both the Legislative Assembly and the Legislative Council).

• Article 170: This article deals with the composition of the Legislative Assemblies, including the number of seats and the delimitation of constituencies.

• Article 171: This article outlines the composition of the Legislative Councils, including the method of election and nomination of members.

• Article 174: This article mandates that the Governor shall summon the Legislature at least once every six months.

• Article 176: This article requires the Governor to address the Legislature at the commencement of the first session after each general election and at the commencement of the first session of each year.

• Article 178: This article provides for the election of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Legislative Assembly.

• Article 194: This article grants certain privileges and immunities to the members of the State Legislature.

• Article 212: This article states that the validity of any proceedings in the Legislature of a state shall not be called in question on the ground of any alleged irregularity of procedure.

q: Which part of Indian Constitution deals with the election of the Vice President?
solution:
The correct answer is Part V.

Key Points

• Part V of the Indian Constitution is titled "The Union".

• It encompasses provisions related to the President, the Vice-President, the Council of Ministers, and the Parliament.

• Articles 52 to 151 deal with the executive, legislative, and administrative functions of the Union Government.

• The election of the Vice President of India is specifically covered under Articles 63 to 71 in Part V of the Constitution.

Additional Information

• Part IV

• Part IV of the Indian Constitution is titled "Directive Principles of State Policy".

• It contains Articles 36 to 51.

• These articles guide the State in making laws and policies to establish a just society in the country.

• However, they are non-justiciable, meaning they are not enforceable by any court.

• Part III

• Part III of the Indian Constitution is titled "Fundamental Rights".

• It contains Articles 12 to 35.

• These articles guarantee essential rights such as equality, freedom, and protection against exploitation.

• These rights are justiciable, meaning they can be enforced by the courts.

• Part VI

• Part VI of the Indian Constitution is titled "The States".

• It contains Articles 152 to 237.

• This part deals with the executive, legislative, and administrative structure of the States.

• It outlines the roles and responsibilities of the Governor, State Legislature, and Council of Ministers.

q: Which writ is issued by a high court or supreme court when a lower court has considered a case going beyond its jurisdiction?
solution:
The correct answer is Prohibition.

Key Points

• Prohibition is issued by a higher court to a lower court or tribunal to prevent it from exceeding its jurisdiction or usurping a jurisdiction that it does not possess.

• This writ is used to control the actions of lower courts and ensure that they do not overstep their boundaries.

• The writ of prohibition directs inactivity, ordering the lower court or tribunal to stop the proceedings in a case that falls outside its jurisdiction.

• It is a form of judicial control over the lower courts by the higher courts like the High Courts and the Supreme Court in India.

Additional Information

• Quo Warranto

• This writ is issued to inquire into the legality of a claim of a person to a public office. It restrains a person from acting in a public office to which they are not entitled.

• The purpose is to prevent illegal usurpation of public office by an individual.

• Habeas Corpus

• This writ is issued to produce a person who has been detained, whether in prison or private custody, before a court and to release that person if such detention is found illegal.

• The primary objective is to ensure the personal liberty of citizens against unlawful detention.

• Certiorari

• This writ is issued by a higher court to a lower court or tribunal to transfer a case pending with the latter to itself or to quash the order of the latter in a case.

• It is issued on grounds of excess of jurisdiction or lack of jurisdiction or error of law apparent on the face of the record.

q: Who among the following was the shortest-serving Prime Minister of India?
solution:
The correct answer is Gulzarilal Nanda.

Key Points

• Gulzarilal Nanda served as the acting Prime Minister of India twice, each time for a short period.

• His first term was from 27th May 1964 to 9th June 1964, following the death of Jawaharlal Nehru.

• His second term was from 11th January 1966 to 24th January 1966, following the death of Lal Bahadur Shastri.

• Both terms combined make him the shortest-serving Prime Minister of India, with a total of 26 days in office.

Additional Information

• Prime Minister of India

• The Prime Minister of India is the head of government and is appointed by the President of India.

• The Prime Minister leads the executive branch of the Government of India and is the chief advisor to the President.

• The Prime Minister also heads the Council of Ministers and is responsible for running the government and implementing policies.

• Acting Prime Minister

• An Acting Prime Minister is appointed when the incumbent Prime Minister is temporarily unable to perform duties, often due to death or resignation.

• Gulzarilal Nanda served as Acting Prime Minister twice under these circumstances.

• Jawaharlal Nehru

• Jawaharlal Nehru was the first Prime Minister of India, serving from 1947 until his death in 1964.

• His death led to Gulzarilal Nanda's first term as Acting Prime Minister.

• Lal Bahadur Shastri

• Lal Bahadur Shastri was the second Prime Minister of India, serving from 1964 until his death in 1966.

• His death led to Gulzarilal Nanda's second term as Acting Prime Minister.

q: Which of the following Constitutional Amendment Acts made the president bound by the advice of the council of ministers headed by the prime minister?
solution:
The correct answer is 42nd.

Key Points

• The 42nd Amendment Act, also known as the "Mini-Constitution," was enacted in 1976 during the Emergency period.

• This amendment made it mandatory for the President of India to act in accordance with the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister.

• The amendment added the words "shall, in the exercise of his functions, act in accordance with such advice" to Article 74(1) of the Indian Constitution.

• This move was aimed at reducing the discretionary powers of the President and ensuring the supremacy of the parliamentary system of government.

Additional Information

• 42nd Amendment Act

• The 42nd Amendment Act is one of the most comprehensive amendments to the Indian Constitution, making significant changes to various parts of the document.

• It attempted to reduce the independence of the judiciary and included provisions to curtail the power of the Supreme Court and High Courts.

• This amendment also added words like "Socialist," "Secular," and "Integrity" to the Preamble of the Indian Constitution.

• The 42nd Amendment is often criticized for its attempt to centralize power and limit the role of state governments.

• Article 74

• Article 74 of the Indian Constitution deals with the Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President.

• Initially, the President had the discretion to reject the advice of the Council of Ministers.

• The 42nd Amendment Act removed this discretion, making the President bound to act on the advice.

• It ensures the President acts as a ceremonial head, with real executive power vested in the Council of Ministers.

• Constitutional Amendments

• Constitutional amendments are changes made to the Constitution to address emerging needs and challenges.

• They require a special majority in both Houses of Parliament and, in certain cases, ratification by at least half of the state legislatures.

• Amendments can be proposed by either the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha.

• Significant amendments often reflect major shifts in the country's political and social landscape.

• Emergency Period (1975-1977)

• The Emergency period in India was from 1975 to 1977, declared by then Prime Minister Indira Gandhi.

• It involved the suspension of elections, curtailment of civil liberties, and increased centralization of power.

• The period is marked by widespread political repression and controversial constitutional changes.

• The 42nd Amendment Act is one of the key legislative changes made during this period.

q: In which of the following cases did the Supreme Court direct that, 'the Parliament cannot take away or abridge any of the fundamental rights for the Implementation of Directive Principles'?
solution:
The correct answer is Golak Nath Case, 1967.

Key Points

• The Golak Nath Case (1967) was a landmark ruling by the Supreme Court of India.

• In this case, the Supreme Court held that the Parliament could not amend the Fundamental Rights enshrined in the Constitution.

• The judgment stated that Fundamental Rights are transcendental and immutable, thus, they cannot be abridged or taken away by any amendment of the Constitution.

• The decision in Golak Nath Case was later overruled by the Kesavananda Bharati Case in 1973, which introduced the Basic Structure Doctrine.

Additional Information

• Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973)

• This case is known for the Basic Structure Doctrine which asserts that certain fundamental features of the Constitution cannot be altered by any amendment.

• The judgment provided stability to the Constitution by ensuring its core values remain intact.

• Minerva Mills Case (1980)

• This case reinforced the Basic Structure Doctrine and further strengthened judicial review.

• The Supreme Court ruled that the power of judicial review is an essential feature of the Constitution.

• Indira Sawhney Case (1992)

• This case is also known as the Mandal Commission Case, which addressed the issue of reservations in government jobs.

• The Supreme Court upheld the 27% reservation for OBCs but excluded the creamy layer.

• Directive Principles of State Policy

• These are guidelines for the framing of laws by the government, set out in Part IV of the Constitution.

• They are non-justiciable in nature, meaning they are not legally enforceable by the courts for their violation.

q: In which of the following cases did the Supreme court of India give a ruling that, 'in case of any conflict between the fundamental rights and the directive principles, the former would prevail'?
solution:
Method:
1. Identify the core conflict: Fundamental Rights (FR) vs. Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP).
2. Recall the early constitutional era (1950s) where FRs were given absolute supremacy.
3. Match the era and ruling to the Champakam Dorairajan Case (1951).

Explanation:
In the Champakam Dorairajan Case (1951), the Supreme Court held that Directive Principles are subsidiary to Fundamental Rights. The court ruled that if a law implementing a DPSP violates a Fundamental Right, the Fundamental Right would prevail. This case eventually led to the First Amendment of the Constitution to allow for certain social reforms.

Why the others are wrong:
(B) Kesavananda Bharati Case established the Basic Structure Doctrine.
(C) Golaknath Case ruled that Fundamental Rights cannot be amended or diluted.
(D) Minerva Mills Case established a "harmony" between FRs and DPSPs, stating they are two wheels of a chariot.

q: Which of the following is NOT the qualification for the appointment of judges of supreme court?
options: An advocate of high court for at least ten years
A distinguished judge in the opinion of the President
A judge of high court for at least five years
An advocate of supreme court for at least ten years
solution:
The correct answer is An advocate of supreme court for at least ten years.

Key Points

• According to the Indian Constitution, the qualifications for appointment as a judge of the Supreme Court are outlined in Article 124.

• An individual must be a judge of one or more High Courts for at least five years.

• Alternatively, an individual should have been an advocate of a High Court for at least ten years.

• The person can also be deemed a distinguished jurist in the opinion of the President of India.

• Being an advocate of the Supreme Court for ten years is not a recognized qualification for appointment as a Supreme Court judge.

Additional Information

• Article 124 of the Indian Constitution

• It deals with the establishment and constitution of the Supreme Court of India.

• It prescribes the qualifications, appointment, and tenure of the judges of the Supreme Court.

• Appointment of Judges

• The President of India appoints the judges of the Supreme Court.

• The Chief Justice of India is appointed by the President after consultation with other judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts as deemed necessary.

• Tenure of Judges

• Supreme Court judges hold office until they attain the age of 65 years.

• They may resign by writing to the President or can be removed by the President on grounds of proven misbehavior or incapacity.

• Removal of Judges

• A judge of the Supreme Court can be removed by an order of the President only after an address by each House of Parliament supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting.

• This process is known as 'impeachment'.

q: Which of the following most accurately describes the legal character of the right to property under Article 300A of the Indian Constitution?
options: It is a fundamental right that guarantees compensation for all property acquisitions.
It allows the State to deprive a person of property by any law, even without due process.
It is a constitutional legal right that permits deprivation only by authority of law.
It permits citizens to claim property protection under Article 32 before the Supreme Court.
solution:

Key Points

• Under Article 300A of the Indian Constitution, the right to property is no longer a fundamental right. It was demoted to a constitutional legal right by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978.

• This article states that no person shall be deprived of their property except by the authority of law.

• This ensures that property can only be taken by the state through a legally established process, providing protection against arbitrary deprivation.

• As a constitutional legal right, this provision primarily ensures that property rights are safeguarded as long as the deprivation occurs through proper legislation.

• Unlike fundamental rights, violations of Article 300A cannot be directly challenged under Article 32 in the Supreme Court.

• However, if property is taken away without following the due process of law, remedies can be sought through the High Courts under Article 226 or other legal avenues.

• The transformation of the right to property from fundamental to constitutional legal right reflects the state's ability to regulate property for public welfare, subject to legal procedures.

• It is a fundamental right that guarantees compensation for all property acquisitions.

• It permits citizens to claim property protection under Article 32 before the Supreme Court.

• Property rights under Article 300A cannot be enforced through Article 32, as they are not fundamental rights. Remedies for violations must be sought through High Courts under Article 226 or other legal mechanisms.

q: Education is now placed under which list after the 42nd Amendment?
