q: Article 370, which granted special status to Jammu and Kashmir, was abrogated by which constitutional mechanism?
solution:
The correct answer is Presidential Order under Article 370(3).

Key Points

• Article 370 granted special status to Jammu and Kashmir, providing autonomy over its internal matters except for defense, foreign affairs, finance, and communications.

• The abrogation of Article 370 was executed using a Presidential Order issued under Article 370(3), which allowed the President of India to make modifications or exceptions to Article 370.

• The Presidential Order C.O. 272, issued on 5th August 2019, replaced the previous Presidential Order from 1954, extending all provisions of the Indian Constitution to Jammu and Kashmir.

• The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganization Act, 2019, was passed by Parliament, bifurcating Jammu and Kashmir into two Union Territories: Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.

• The procedure involved obtaining the concurrence of the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly, which was absent at the time due to President's Rule. Consequently, the concurrence was given by the Governor, who was acting on behalf of the state legislature.

Additional Information

• Article 370:

• Article 370 was part of the Indian Constitution that provided special autonomy to Jammu and Kashmir.

• It was incorporated as a temporary provision under Part XXI of the Constitution, which deals with “Temporary, Transitional, and Special Provisions.”

• Under Article 370, the state had its own Constitution and decision-making rights in all matters except defense, foreign affairs, finance, and communications.

• It also allowed Jammu and Kashmir to have a separate flag and denied property rights to outsiders.

• Presidential Order and Article 370(3):

• Article 370(3) empowered the President of India to declare Article 370 inoperative or modify it, provided the recommendation of the Constituent Assembly of Jammu and Kashmir was obtained.

• Since the Constituent Assembly of Jammu and Kashmir ceased to exist in 1957, the Indian government used the provision of President's Rule in the state to bypass this requirement.

• The Presidential Order issued on 5th August 2019 extended all provisions of the Indian Constitution to Jammu and Kashmir, effectively nullifying its special status.

• Jammu and Kashmir Reorganization Act, 2019:

• Passed on 6th August 2019, this Act reorganized the state of Jammu and Kashmir into two Union Territories: Jammu and Kashmir (with a Legislative Assembly) and Ladakh (without a Legislative Assembly).

• The Act came into effect on 31st October 2019.

• The bifurcation aimed to improve governance and integrate the region fully with the rest of India.

• Impact of Abrogation:

• The abrogation of Article 370 has led to the extension of all Indian laws and provisions to Jammu and Kashmir.

• It has sparked debates on federalism, autonomy, and the rights of states under the Indian Constitution.

• While some argue it has brought greater integration, others highlight concerns over political representation and regional identity.

Important Points

• Article 368: This article pertains to the power of Parliament to amend the Constitution, including fundamental rights. However, it was not used for the abrogation of Article 370.

• Article 356: This article allows the imposition of President's Rule in a state due to the failure of constitutional machinery. While President's Rule was in effect in Jammu and Kashmir, Article 356 was not directly used for the abrogation.

• Ordinance by the President: Ordinances are temporary laws issued by the President when Parliament is not in session. This mechanism was not employed for abrogating Article 370.

• It is important to understand that the abrogation of Article 370 followed a unique constitutional process, combining Presidential Orders and Parliamentary legislation.

q: Which of the following is true about Fundamental Rights and DPSPs?
options: Both are justiciable and enforceable by courts
DPSPs override Fundamental Rights when in conflict
Fundamental Rights are justiciable, but DPSPs are not
DPSPs are guaranteed by the Constitution;Fundamental Rights are optional
solution:
The Correct answer is Fundamental Rights are justiciable, but DPSPs are not.

Key Points

• Fundamental Rights are explicitly mentioned in Part III of the Indian Constitution.

• They are enforceable by the courts, meaning individuals can approach the courts if their rights are violated. This makes them justiciable.

• The Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSPs), enshrined in Part IV of the Constitution, are not enforceable by the courts, making them non-justiciable.

• DPSPs act as guidelines for the government to achieve socio-economic goals and establish a welfare state.

• While Fundamental Rights focus on individual rights and liberties, DPSPs emphasize collective welfare and societal development.

• The Supreme Court of India has clarified that Fundamental Rights and DPSPs must be harmonized and not seen as conflicting entities.

• Examples of Fundamental Rights include the Right to Equality (Article 14-18) and the Right to Freedom (Article 19-22).

• Examples of DPSPs include the directive to promote equal justice and free legal aid (Article 39A) and to ensure living wages for workers (Article 43).

Additional Information

• Both are justiciable and enforceable by courts

• This option is incorrect because only Fundamental Rights are enforceable by courts, while DPSPs are not.

• DPSPs serve as principles for governance and cannot be legally upheld in courts.

• DPSPs override Fundamental Rights when in conflict

• The Supreme Court has ruled that Fundamental Rights hold a higher position in cases of conflict.

• However, efforts have been made to harmonize both, recognizing their complementary nature.

• DPSPs are guaranteed by the Constitution; Fundamental Rights are optional

• This is incorrect as both Fundamental Rights and DPSPs are integral parts of the Constitution.

• Fundamental Rights are guaranteed and enforceable, while DPSPs are guidelines that cannot be enforced legally.

q: The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) places emphasis on the use of technology to ensure the authenticity of evidence. This is particularly relevant for:
solution:
The correct answer is Digital and electronic evidence.

Key Points

• The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), or the Indian Evidence Act, emphasizes the importance of using technology to ensure the authenticity and reliability of evidence.

• It is particularly relevant for digital and electronic evidence, as such evidence can be tampered with or altered without proper mechanisms to ensure its integrity.

• Digital evidence includes data obtained from electronic devices such as computers, smartphones, hard drives, and cloud-based storage systems. Examples include emails, SMS messages, call logs, and CCTV footage.

• The Act includes provisions for the admissibility of electronic records under Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, where certified electronic records are treated as evidence in courts.

• This emphasis on technology aligns with global judicial trends where digital evidence plays a crucial role in solving crimes ranging from cybercrimes to financial fraud and organized crime.

Additional Information

• Digital and Electronic Evidence:

• It includes all forms of evidence that are stored or transmitted in a digital format. Examples: emails, social media posts, digital documents, and server logs.

• Key features: It is highly prone to tampering, requires proper authentication, and necessitates the use of advanced forensic techniques for validation.

• Under Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act, electronic records are treated as valid evidence if they meet certain technical criteria, like certification by a responsible official.

• Physical Exhibits:

• This refers to tangible objects obtained from crime scenes, such as weapons, clothing, or fingerprints.

• Physical evidence is crucial but is not typically subject to the same scrutiny as digital evidence in terms of authenticity checks because of its material nature.

• Hand-Written Diaries:

• This type of evidence is considered under traditional documentary evidence and does not involve technology for validation.

• Handwriting experts may be used for authentication.

• Oral Confessions:

• These are verbal statements made by a suspect or accused during interrogation.

• Such evidence is admissible under Indian law but must be corroborated with other evidence to ensure reliability.

• Admissibility of Digital Evidence Globally:

• The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) has emphasized the importance of digital evidence in combating transnational crimes.

• Countries like the USA and the UK also have laws in place, such as the Federal Rules of Evidence in the USA, that govern the admissibility of digital evidence.

Important Points

• Section 65B Certification: A certificate is required for the admissibility of electronic records, which ensures that the evidence was generated and stored in a reliable manner.

• Electronic Evidence Forensics: Advanced forensic tools are used to extract and analyze data while maintaining its integrity.

• Challenges: The dynamic nature of digital evidence, jurisdictional issues (e.g., data stored overseas), and encryption can complicate its use in legal proceedings.

• Role in Modern Crimes: Digital evidence is indispensable in solving cybercrimes, financial fraud, and even traditional crimes where technology plays a role, such as using CCTV footage in robbery cases.

• Judicial Precedents: Indian courts have increasingly relied on digital evidence, with landmark cases such as Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer (2014) setting important precedents for admissibility.

q: Which of the following changes has Bharatiya Nagarik suraksha Samhita(BNSS) brought to criminal procedure?
solution:
The correct answer is Video-recorded confessions.

Key Points

• Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Samhita (BNSS) replaces the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), focusing on modernizing criminal procedure laws in India to align with contemporary requirements.

• The introduction of video-recorded confessions ensures transparency and enhances the reliability of evidence presented in courts. This provision aims to eliminate coercion and safeguard the rights of the accused.

• The initiative reflects a move toward digitization and technological integration in judicial processes, ensuring accountability and reducing malpractices.

• BNSS does not include provisions like presumption of guilt or scrapping of bail rights, as these would violate fundamental rights under the Constitution of India. Hence, these statements are incorrect.

• BNSS does not replace all IPC sections. It specifically deals with procedures rather than substantive criminal laws. Hence, this statement is also incorrect.

• *Hence, the correct answer is video-recorded confessions.*

Additional Information

• Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Samhita (BNSS):

• The BNSS, enacted in 2023, aims to enhance efficiency in criminal procedures and ensure justice delivery in a time-bound manner.

• The law emphasizes digital integration, including the use of technology for evidence recording, case management, and monitoring judicial processes.

• The BNSS also facilitates victim-centric justice by ensuring their active participation in the legal process and introducing provisions for victim compensation.

• Video-recorded confessions:

• This provision is aligned with global best practices, enhancing the credibility of the judicial system and ensuring compliance with Article 21 of the Constitution, which guarantees the right to life and personal liberty.

• It addresses concerns related to custodial torture or forced confessions by ensuring that statements are recorded in a transparent and impartial manner.

• Key Principles of Criminal Procedure:

• The principles of criminal procedure emphasize fair trial, presumption of innocence, and adherence to fundamental rights.

• BNSS retains these principles, reinforcing the importance of due process and equality before the law.

• Indian Penal Code (IPC):

• The IPC, enacted in 1860, is the primary criminal code in India, addressing substantive criminal law.

• BNSS focuses exclusively on procedures, ensuring streamlined processes for investigation, trial, and sentencing.

• Constitutional Provisions:

• Article 22 protects against arbitrary arrest and detention, ensuring safeguards for the accused during criminal proceedings.

• BNSS aligns with constitutional mandates to uphold justice, transparency, and the rule of law.

Important Points

• Digitization in Criminal Justice:

• The use of technology, such as video recording, reduces the scope for manipulation and ensures transparency in judicial proceedings.

• India's judicial reforms, including BNSS, aim to integrate digital tools to expedite case disposal and improve access to justice.

• International Best Practices:

• Several countries, including the United States and United Kingdom, have implemented video-recorded confessions to ensure the integrity of legal processes.

• India's adoption of such practices reflects its commitment to modernizing its judicial system in line with global standards.

• Victim-Centric Justice:

• BNSS incorporates provisions to ensure timely justice for victims and safeguard their rights during legal proceedings.

• Compensation mechanisms under BNSS aim to reduce the financial burden on victims and their families.

q: Which of the following is true regarding the Anglo-Indian representation in State Assemblies?
options: The Governor still nominates one Anglo-Indian member to the Assembly.
The provision was abolished by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment.
The provision was abolished by the 104th Constitutional Amendment.
Anglo-Indian members are elected through proportional representation.
solution:
The correct answer is The provision was abolished by the 104th Constitutional Amendment..

Key Points

• The Anglo-Indian representation in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies was provided under Article 331 and Article 333 of the Indian Constitution, respectively.

• The 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019, abolished the provision for the nomination of Anglo-Indian members to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies. This amendment came into effect on January 25, 2020.

• The provision for Anglo-Indian representation was initially introduced to provide political representation to a small minority community in India. However, the government reasoned that the Anglo-Indian population had significantly decreased, and there was no longer a need for this special representation.

• Governors of states were earlier empowered to nominate one Anglo-Indian member to the State Legislative Assemblies under Article 333, but this provision was removed by the 104th Amendment.

• Statements in the question:

• Statement 1: "The Governor still nominates one Anglo-Indian member to the Assembly." – Incorrect, as this provision was abolished by the 104th Constitutional Amendment.

• Statement 2: "The provision was abolished by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment." – Incorrect, as the 42nd Amendment (1976) did not deal with Anglo-Indian representation.

• Statement 3: "The provision was abolished by the 104th Constitutional Amendment." – Correct.

• Statement 4: "Anglo-Indian members are elected through proportional representation." – Incorrect, as they were nominated and not elected.

Additional Information

• Anglo-Indian Community:

• Anglo-Indians are a small community in India that originated during the British colonial period, with mixed Indian and European ancestry.

• The community played an important role in India's administration, railways, and education system during British rule.

• 104th Constitutional Amendment Act:

• It abolished the special representation of Anglo-Indians in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies.

• It also extended the reservation for Scheduled Castes (SC) and Scheduled Tribes (ST) in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies for another 10 years.

• Historical Context:

• The Anglo-Indian representation was initially a safeguard for a minority community to voice their concerns in legislative bodies.

• Over time, with the decline in the population of Anglo-Indians and their assimilation into mainstream society, this provision was deemed unnecessary.

• Other Reserved Categories in India:

• Seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes (SC) and Scheduled Tribes (ST) in legislative bodies under Articles 330 and 332 of the Constitution.

• These reservations aim to ensure the political representation of historically disadvantaged communities.

Important Points

• The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act (1976) is often referred to as the "Mini-Constitution" because it introduced significant changes but did not address Anglo-Indian representation.

• The 104th Constitutional Amendment was passed in December 2019 and came into effect on January 25, 2020.

• Currently, no seats are reserved for Anglo-Indians in either the Lok Sabha or State Legislative Assemblies.

• This amendment highlights the dynamic nature of the Constitution, which adapts to social and demographic changes.

q: What change did the Regulating Act bring to the post of the Governor of Bengal?

• The Act also brought the presidencies of Bombay and Madras under the control of the Governor-General of Bengal in matters of war and diplomacy.

• The Regulating Act of 1773 was the first major legislative intervention by the British Parliament in Indian affairs.

• It aimed to reform the administration of the East India Company and ensure better governance in its Indian territories.

• The Act marked the beginning of British parliamentary control over the East India Company's operations in India.

• It also laid the foundation for subsequent acts that gradually centralized British authority in India.

q: Which Article enables the President to establish an Inter-State Council?

• The Inter-State Council promotes coordination and cooperation among the states and the Union of India, ensuring smooth governance and resolving inter-state disputes.

Additional Information

• Article 264:

q: Which of the following correctly reflects the legal implication of Article 255 regarding presidential or governor's assent to bills?
options: State law is void without written Governor assent.
Mention of assent is mandatory for validity.
Omission of prior recommendation doesn't invalidate law if assent is given.
President's assent must precede legislative passage to be valid.
solution:
The correct answer is Omission of prior recommendation doesn't invalidate law if assent is given.

Key Points

• Article 255 of the Indian Constitution states that the absence of prior recommendation or sanction required by the Constitution does not invalidate a law if it has received the assent of the President or the Governor.

• The provision ensures that minor procedural lapses do not obstruct the legislative process, provided the bill has been duly assented to.

• For example, even if a recommendation from the President or Governor is not obtained at the time of introducing a bill, the law remains valid if subsequent assent is granted.

• This article upholds the principle of legislative supremacy by ensuring that procedural errors do not nullify valid legislative acts.

• It applies to both state and central legislation, ensuring uniformity in the treatment of procedural lapses related to assent.

Additional Information

• Constitutional Articles (Part VI, Chapter II)

• Article 153: Establishes the office of the Governor for each state (one person can be Governor for two or more states).

• Article 154: Vests the executive power of the state in the Governor.

• Article 155: Appointment by the President (warrant under hand and seal).

• Article 156: Term of office (holds office during President's pleasure).

• Article 157: Qualifications for appointment (Citizen of India, 35 years old).

• Article 163: Council of Ministers to aid and advise the Governor (except in discretionary matters).

• Article 164: Other provisions as to Ministers (appointment, responsibility to the Assembly).

q: What is the primary objective of a Uniform Civil Code (UCC) in India?
options: To establish a common criminal law for all citizens.

To standardize administrative procedures across all states.
solution:

Key Points

• The Uniform Civil Code (UCC) aims to replace personal laws based on the customs and scriptures of various religious communities with a common set of laws governing marriage, divorce, inheritance, and adoption for all citizens of India.

• The UCC is enshrined as a directive principle under Article 44 of the Indian Constitution, which calls for the State to endeavor to secure a uniform civil code for all citizens.

• It seeks to ensure equality and secularism by eliminating discriminatory practices embedded in personal laws based on religion or gender.

• The implementation of UCC is viewed as a significant step toward achieving gender justice and promoting national integration by ensuring uniformity in legal matters across all communities.

• The Supreme Court of India has, on several occasions, emphasized the need for a Uniform Civil Code to ensure equality and uniformity in personal laws.

Additional Information

• Classification of DPSPs (Philosophical Basis):

• Socialistic Principles: Aim for socio-economic justice, reducing inequality (e.g., equal pay, right to work).

• Gandhian Principles: Promote Gandhian ideals (e.g., village panchayats, cow protection, cottage industries).

• Liberal-Intellectual Principles: Advocate for individual freedoms and state action (e.g., uniform civil code, separation of judiciary from executive).

q: Which section of Bharatiya Nagarik suraksha Samhita(BNSS) mandates video-recording of search and seizure operations?
solution:
The correct answer is Section 105.

Key Points

• Section 105 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Samhita (BNSS) focuses on ensuring transparency and accountability in search and seizure operations conducted by law enforcement agencies.

• It mandates that all search and seizure operations should be video-recorded to ensure there is a clear record of the proceedings.

• The provision is aimed at safeguarding the rights of individuals and preventing any misuse of authority during these operations.

• Video recording serves as evidence in legal proceedings and ensures that the process is conducted fairly and in adherence to the law.

• This provision aligns with the broader objective of reforming criminal laws in India and enhancing trust between the public and law enforcement agencies.

Additional Information

• Section 50:

• Section 50 of BNSS deals with the rights of individuals during search and arrest.

• It mandates that a person being searched has the right to have the search conducted in the presence of two independent witnesses.

• This provision aims to ensure transparency and prevent any misconduct by the authorities during the search process.

• Section 62:

• Section 62 focuses on the procedural guidelines for the arrest of individuals.

• It outlines the rights of the arrested person, such as the right to be informed about the reasons for the arrest and the right to legal representation.

• It ensures that arrests are conducted lawfully and in compliance with the principles of natural justice.

• Section 176:

• Section 176 deals with the investigation of custodial deaths and disappearances.

• It mandates that such cases should be investigated by a judicial magistrate or an executive magistrate to ensure impartiality and accountability.

• This provision is crucial for addressing concerns related to custodial violence and ensuring justice for victims.

• Theme of Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Samhita (BNSS):

• The BNSS is a comprehensive reform of the Indian criminal laws, replacing the colonial-era Indian Penal Code (IPC), Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), and Indian Evidence Act.

• It aims to modernize the criminal justice system, focusing on transparency, accountability, and the protection of citizens' rights.

• The reforms emphasize the use of technology, such as video recording, to enhance the efficiency and fairness of criminal investigations and trials.

q: The President is elected by an electoral college, while the Governor is _.
solution:
The correct answer is Appointed by the President.

Key Points

• The Governor of a state in India is appointed by the President of India under Article 155 of the Indian Constitution.

• The Governor acts as the nominal head of the state, while the real executive powers lie with the Chief Minister and the Council of Ministers.

• The Governor serves a term of 5 years, but they hold office at the pleasure of the President, meaning they can be removed earlier.

• The appointment process ensures that the Governor is a representative of the central government in the state and maintains coordination between the center and state.

• The role of the Governor includes duties such as granting assent to bills, appointing the Chief Minister, and overseeing the formation of the state government after elections.

Additional Information

• Key Appointments by the President:

• Prime Minister (PM) & Council of Ministers: Appoints the PM (usually leader of the majority in Lok Sabha) and other ministers on the PM's advice.

• Judiciary: Chief Justice of India, Supreme Court Judges, and High Court Judges (on consultation).

• Election Commission: Chief Election Commissioner and other Commissioners.

• Union Public Service Commission (UPSC): Chairman and Members.

• Attorney General of India: The government's chief legal advisor.

• Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG): Guardian of public finances.

• Governors: Appointed for each state.

• Administrators: For Union Territories.

• National Commissions: Chairpersons & members for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, Minorities, etc.

q:
Consider the following statements:

1. The Governor can dissolve the State Legislative Assembly.

2. The President has no such power regarding the Lok Sabha. Which of the above is/are correct?
solution:
The correct answer is Option 1: Only 1.

Key Points

• The Governor of a state has the constitutional authority to dissolve the State Legislative Assembly under Article 174(2)(b) of the Indian Constitution, usually on the advice of the Chief Minister or in certain circumstances like a no-confidence motion.

• The President of India, on the other hand, has the power to dissolve the Lok Sabha under Article 85(2)(b) of the Indian Constitution. Therefore, Statement 2 is incorrect.

• The dissolution of the State Legislative Assembly is an executive action of the Governor and is generally done to pave the way for fresh elections.

• The President's power to dissolve the Lok Sabha is exercised on the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister.

• Thus, only Statement 1 is correct, as the Governor has the power to dissolve the State Legislative Assembly.

Additional Information

• Governor's Role and Powers:

• The Governor is the constitutional head of the state and acts on the advice of the state's Chief Minister and Council of Ministers.

• The Governor can summon, prorogue, or dissolve the State Legislative Assembly under Article 174 of the Constitution.

• In extraordinary circumstances (e.g., no-confidence motion passed), the Governor can dissolve the assembly without the advice of the Chief Minister, but this is subject to judicial review.

• President's Power to Dissolve Lok Sabha:

• The President of India can dissolve the Lok Sabha under Article 85(2)(b) of the Constitution.

• This power is exercised on the advice of the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers.

• The dissolution of the Lok Sabha paves the way for general elections in the country.

• Difference Between Dissolution and Prorogation:

• Dissolution: Refers to the complete termination of the current House of Parliament or State Legislative Assembly. It necessitates fresh elections.

• Prorogation: Refers to the termination of a session of the House without dissolving it. It simply ends the proceedings for the session.

q: Fill in the blanks: The Parliament can create a new All-India Service by a resolution in the _.
solution:
The correct answer is Rajya Sabha.

Key Points

• Under Article 312 of the Indian Constitution, the Parliament can create a new All-India Service by passing a resolution in the Rajya Sabha.

• The resolution must be passed by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting in the Rajya Sabha.

• After the Rajya Sabha passes the resolution, the Parliament enacts legislation to officially create the new All-India Service.

• All-India Services include the Indian Administrative Service (IAS), Indian Police Service (IPS), and Indian Forest Service (IFS), among others.

• These services are unique as they are recruited and trained centrally but serve both the central and state governments, ensuring uniformity in administrative practices across the nation.

Additional Information

• Lok Sabha

• The Lok Sabha, also known as the House of the People, is the lower house of the Indian Parliament.

• It plays a crucial role in the legislative process, particularly in financial matters, as money bills can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha.

• State Assemblies

• State Assemblies, or Vidhan Sabhas, are the legislative bodies of individual states in India.

• They are responsible for making laws on state subjects as listed in the State List of the Constitution.

• GST Council

• The GST Council is a constitutional body under Article 279A, responsible for making decisions related to the Goods and Services Tax (GST).

• It is chaired by the Union Finance Minister and includes representatives from all states and union territories.

q:
Arrange the following steps in the correct legislative process for the passage of a Money Bill in India:

A) Introduction of Money Bill in Lok Sabha

B) Passage in Lok Sabha

C) Transmission to Rajya Sabha

D) Presentation for President's assent
solution:
The correct answer is Option 1: A-B-C-D.

Key Points

• In India, a Money Bill is exclusively introduced in the Lok Sabha, as per Article 110 of the Constitution of India.

• Once introduced, the Money Bill must be passed by the Lok Sabha, where the majority support is required.

• After passage in the Lok Sabha, the bill is transmitted to the Rajya Sabha for its recommendations, but the Rajya Sabha cannot amend or reject the bill; it can only suggest changes within 14 days.

• Finally, the bill is presented to the President of India for his/her assent, which is mandatory for the bill to become a law.

• The process ensures that the Lok Sabha, as the house of elected representatives, has the final say in matters related to financial legislation.

Additional Information

• Important Facts about Money Bills:

• A bill is considered a Money Bill if it deals with taxation, borrowing of money by the government, appropriation of money out of the Consolidated Fund of India, or any matter incidental to these issues.

• The Speaker of the Lok Sabha has the final authority to decide whether a bill is a Money Bill or not.

• The Rajya Sabha cannot reject or amend a Money Bill but can suggest recommendations, which the Lok Sabha may choose to accept or reject.

• If the Rajya Sabha does not return the Money Bill within 14 days, it is deemed to have been passed by both houses in the form originally passed by the Lok Sabha.

q: Which of the following commissions recommended the establishment of a Permanent Secretariat for the Inter-State Council to institutionalize Centre-State cooperation?
solution:
The correct answer is Sarkaria Commission.

Key Points

• The Sarkaria Commission was established by the Government of India in June 1983 to review the Centre-State relations.

• It recommended the establishment of a Permanent Secretariat for the Inter-State Council to institutionalize Centre-State cooperation.

• The Inter-State Council is a constitutional body under Article 263 of the Indian Constitution to investigate and discuss subjects of common interest between the Union and States.

• The Sarkaria Commission emphasized the need for better communication and coordination between the Centre and States to strengthen federalism in India.

• Its recommendations led to the formation of the Inter-State Council in 1990, which serves as an important platform for resolving disputes and promoting cooperative federalism.

Additional Information

• Rajamannar Committee

• It was set up by the Tamil Nadu government in 1969 under the chairmanship of P.V. Rajamannar.

• The committee recommended more autonomy to states and a redefinition of Centre-State relations.

• It suggested the abolition of the Planning Commission, the discontinuation of All India Services, and the transfer of subjects from the Union List to the State List.

• However, its recommendations were not implemented at the national level.

• Punchhi Commission

• The Punchhi Commission was set up in April 2007 under the chairmanship of Justice M.M. Punchhi to look into Centre-State relations.

• It recommended a fixed term for Governors, a comprehensive framework for disaster management, and changes to the role of the Governor in state politics.

• It focused on addressing challenges to federalism in the context of globalization and socio-economic changes.

• Its report is considered significant for improving Centre-State relations but is yet to be fully implemented.

• Venkatachelliah Commission

• Also known as the National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution (NCRWC), it was established in 2000 under Justice M.N. Venkatachaliah.

• The commission aimed to review the Constitution to make it more effective and relevant in contemporary times.

• It suggested reforms in electoral processes, judicial accountability, and the functioning of parliamentary institutions.

• It did not specifically focus on Centre-State relations or the Inter-State Council.

q: Article 246A of the Constitution of India gives power to both Parliament and State Legislatures to make laws on .
solution:
The correct answer is Taxation of Goods and Services.

Key Points

• Article 246A of the Indian Constitution was introduced through the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016, which enabled the implementation of the Goods and Services Tax (GST).

• It grants concurrent powers to both the Parliament and State Legislatures to make laws with respect to GST.

• Under this article, the Parliament has exclusive power to make laws on inter-state trade or commerce of goods and services, while both Parliament and State Legislatures can legislate on intra-state transactions.

• GST subsumes multiple indirect taxes such as VAT, Service Tax, Excise Duty, and others, simplifying India's indirect taxation system.

• The introduction of Article 246A aimed to promote a unified market, enhance ease of doing business, and eliminate the cascading effects of taxes.

Additional Information

• Property Rights (Option 1):

• Property rights in India are addressed under Article 300A of the Indian Constitution, which states that no person shall be deprived of their property except by the authority of law.

• Initially, property rights were a fundamental right under Article 31, but it was abolished by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978, and made a legal right under Article 300A.

• This provision ensures that private property cannot be taken away without due process of law or proper compensation.

• Emergency Provisions (Option 3):

• Emergency provisions are detailed under Part XVIII (Articles 352 to 360) of the Indian Constitution.

• These provisions enable the government to assume greater control during times of crisis and include three types of emergencies: National Emergency (Article 352), State Emergency/President’s Rule (Article 356), and Financial Emergency (Article 360).

• These provisions are invoked to safeguard the sovereignty, unity, and integrity of India during extraordinary situations.

• Criminal Law (Option 4):

• Criminal law in India is primarily governed by the Indian Penal Code (IPC), 1860, the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), 1973, and various special laws.

• The Parliament and state legislatures can legislate on criminal law under the Concurrent List (List III) of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution.

• Criminal law ensures the maintenance of public order, punishment for offenses, and the protection of citizens’ rights.

q: Under Article 262 of the Indian Constitution, which of the following interpretations most accurately reflects Parliament's authority regarding inter-State water disputes?
options: Legislate on river navigation but not bar SC jurisdiction
Set up tribunals for water disputes and bar SC review
Mandate ISC mediation before court action
solution:
The correct answer is Set up tribunals for water disputes and bar SC review.

Key Points

• Under Article 262 of the Indian Constitution, Parliament has the authority to legislate for the adjudication of inter-State water disputes.

• The provision explicitly allows Parliament to bar the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court or any other court in such disputes by creating specialized mechanisms like tribunals.

• In accordance with Article 262, the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act (1956) was enacted, which empowers the Union Government to establish tribunals for resolving inter-State water disputes.

• Tribunals constituted under this act are the highest authority for adjudicating water disputes, with no provision for judicial review by the Supreme Court to ensure quicker resolution.

• The purpose of this constitutional arrangement is to avoid legal delays and ensure impartial resolution of disputes through a focused mechanism.

Additional Information

• Inter-State Water Disputes

• Inter-State water disputes arise when States disagree over sharing, usage, or control of river waters flowing across their boundaries.

• Article 262 of the Constitution provides a framework for resolving these disputes through legislation and tribunals.

• Such disputes are handled under the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, ensuring legal and administrative mechanisms for resolution without judicial delays.

q: The Bharatiya Nyaya Samhita (BNS), 2023, consolidates and amends provisions related to which branch of law?
solution:
The correct answer is Criminal Substantive Law.

Key Points

• The Bharatiya Nyaya Samhita (BNS), 2023, is aimed at consolidating and amending laws related to Criminal Substantive Law in India.

• BNS is designed as a replacement for the Indian Penal Code (IPC), 1860, which was drafted during British colonial rule in India.

• The primary objective of the BNS is to modernize and reform criminal laws to align with the changing socio-economic and technological landscape of the country.

• It seeks to simplify criminal laws, ensure speedy justice, and address contemporary challenges such as cybercrime and organized crime.

• The Bharatiya Nyaya Samhita Bill, 2023, was introduced in Parliament in August 2023 as part of a broader initiative to overhaul colonial-era legal frameworks, including the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) and the Indian Evidence Act.

Additional Information

• Civil Procedure Law

• Civil Procedure Law governs the procedures and practices in civil courts, such as filing lawsuits, conducting trials, and enforcing judgments.

• The primary legislation governing this branch in India is the Civil Procedure Code (CPC), 1908.

• Civil laws deal with private disputes between individuals or organizations, such as property disputes, contracts, or family matters.

• Evidence Law

• The law of evidence deals with the rules and principles that determine what evidence is admissible in courts.

• The Indian Evidence Act, 1872, is the governing framework for evidence-related matters in Indian courts.

• It specifies the type and manner of evidence that can be presented in civil or criminal cases, including oral, documentary, and circumstantial evidence.

• Contract Law

• Contract law governs agreements between parties that are enforceable by law.

• The primary legislation in India is the Indian Contract Act, 1872, which outlines the essentials of a valid contract, including offer, acceptance, consideration, and capacity to contract.

• It also covers specific contracts such as indemnity, guarantee, bailment, agency, and partnership agreements.

q: Bharatiya Nagarik suraksha Samhita(BNSS) ensures access to FIR through which portal?
solution:
The correct answer is CCTNS.

Key Points

• Crime and Criminal Tracking Network and Systems (CCTNS) is a comprehensive and integrated system for effective policing through e-Governance.

• It was launched by the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), Government of India, in 2009 as part of the national e-governance initiative.

• CCTNS facilitates a nationwide networked infrastructure for tracking crime and criminals in real-time, ensuring seamless sharing of information between police stations and higher police authorities.

• The system also enables citizens to access police services such as lodging FIRs, tracking case status, and obtaining verification certificates online.

• As of now, most states and union territories in India use the CCTNS platform to provide services like digital filing of FIRs, improving transparency and efficiency in policing activities.

Additional Information

• National Crime Portal

• It is not a specific portal but often refers to platforms like the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) website.

• The NCRB is responsible for collecting and analyzing crime data as mandated by the Ministry of Home Affairs but does not directly allow citizens to lodge FIRs.

• BHAVISHYA

• BHAVISHYA is an online Pension Sanction and Payment Tracking System launched by the Government of India.

• It is designed to cater to retiring employees for tracking their pension process, ensuring transparency and timely disbursal.

• This portal is unrelated to crime or police services.

• DIGI-FIR

• DIGI-FIR is a concept introduced in some states like Madhya Pradesh to allow citizens to lodge FIRs online.

• While it serves a similar purpose, it is not implemented nationwide or as comprehensively as CCTNS.

• Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Samhita (BNSS)

• The BNSS is a proposed draft legislation aimed at replacing the existing Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) to modernize and streamline the criminal justice system in India.

• One of its key features is enabling citizens to access FIRs and other police services online, which aligns with the goals of CCTNS.

q:
Consider the following statements:

1. Every Money Bill is a Financial Bill.

2. Every Financial Bill is a Money Bill.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution:
The correct answer is Option 1.

Key Points

• A Money Bill is a specific type of Financial Bill under Article 110 of the Indian Constitution.

• Every Money Bill is a Financial Bill because it contains provisions exclusively dealing with financial matters such as taxation, borrowing, expenditure, or other money-related issues.

• However, not every Financial Bill is a Money Bill. Financial Bills can also include provisions beyond the scope of Article 110, requiring approval from both Houses of Parliament.

• A Money Bill can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha and requires the certification of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.

• Thus, Statement 1 is correct, and Statement 2 is incorrect, making Option 1 the correct answer.

Additional Information

• Money Bill:

• A Money Bill is defined under Article 110 of the Indian Constitution.

• It contains provisions exclusively related to taxes, borrowing of money by the government, withdrawal of money from the Consolidated Fund or Contingency Fund, and appropriation of funds.

• It must be introduced in the Lok Sabha with the recommendation of the President.

• The Rajya Sabha can suggest amendments but cannot amend or reject a Money Bill. It has to return the bill to the Lok Sabha within 14 days.

• Financial Bill:

• Financial Bills are broader in scope and include Money Bills as a subset. There are two types of Financial Bills:

• Category A: These contain provisions related to financial matters and provisions not covered under Article 110. They need the President's recommendation and must be introduced in the Lok Sabha.

• Category B: These involve only incidental financial provisions and do not require the President's recommendation.

q:
Read the below statement:

1. Solicitor General of India is appointed by the president of India.

2. A candidate contesting for the post of the President of India is required to make a security deposit of ₹15,000.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution:
The correct answer is Only statement 2.

Key Points

• The security deposit of ₹15,000 is mandatory for candidates contesting the election for the President of India, as per Article 58 of the Constitution of India and the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952.

• The deposit is forfeited if the candidate fails to secure at least one-sixth of the votes cast in the election.

• The security deposit ensures that only serious candidates participate in the election process.

• The election of the President of India is conducted by an electoral college consisting of elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the Legislative Assemblies of States and Union Territories.

• As per the rules, the nomination paper must be supported by at least 50 proposers and 50 seconders to ensure legitimacy.

Additional Information

• Statement 1: Solicitor General of India is appointed by the president of India

• The Solicitor General of India is the second-highest law officer in the country after the Attorney General of India.

• Unlike the Attorney General, the Solicitor General is not appointed directly by the President of India. Instead, the appointment is made by the Union Government, specifically by the Ministry of Law and Justice.

• The Solicitor General assists the Attorney General in performing legal duties and advises the government on legal matters.

• Therefore, Statement 1 is incorrect.

• Concept of Presidential Elections in India:

• The President is elected by an electoral college through a proportional representation system using a single transferable vote.

• Every member of the electoral college casts their vote, and the candidate receiving the highest number of votes is elected.

• The process is governed by the provisions in Articles 52 to 62 of the Constitution.

• Other Important Facts:

• The President of India serves a term of five years and can be re-elected.

• The eligibility criteria for candidates contesting the Presidential elections include being a citizen of India, at least 35 years old, and qualified to be a member of the Lok Sabha.

• In case of vacancy, the election must be held within six months.
